own.reply: A house on the hill with a dog, a view of the ridge road and my grandfather’s rifle in a locked cabinet. He was the fire warden. I’ve never fired it. I keep it oiled for him.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What does your dad do?
own.reply: He was a logger until the logging went. Then the ridge’s quarry. He came back with a cough and a quiet. He won’t say what they quarry up there.

calls.label: Ask what was beside the bear prints
calls.player: Was there anything else by the bear prints?
calls.reply: Boot prints and a van’s tyre marks, which I didn’t tell the children. The fence had been cut and mended. Somebody tried to take that bear off our playing field. I’ve seen a van with no plates on the hill road twice, at dawn, going up.
calls.note: Heather Collins found boot prints, tyre marks and a cut fence beside the bear prints at the hill school.

calls.label: Ask about a child’s drawing
calls.player: Has a child ever drawn something that worried you?
calls.reply: A six-year-old whose father works on the ridge drew a man in a cloak reading to his dad at a gate. I kept the drawing. Children draw what they see. That’s the frightening bit.
calls.note: Heather Collins has a child’s drawing of a man in a cloak reading to a worker at a gate on the ridge.

own.label: Ask about art school
own.player: What’s art school like?
own.reply: Everyone makes installations about their feelings. I paint landscapes. They think I’m a reactionary.

own.label: Ask why she paints landscapes
own.player: Why landscapes, when everyone else does installations?
own.reply: Because the desert is beautiful and my classmates are not. Beauty isn’t old-fashioned. It’s just hard.

own.label: Ask what she sketched
own.player: Have you sketched anything strange lately?
own.reply: I sketch the old chapel at night for the light. Last time there were people inside, in a circle. I drew them before I got scared.
own.note: Chloe Farrow sketched people standing in a circle inside the old chapel at night.

own.label: Ask what she thinks art is for
own.player: What do you think art is for?
own.reply: Beauty. I know that’s unfashionable. My tutors want everything to be a statement. A sunset isn’t a statement. It’s just true.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Who taught you to paint?
own.reply: My dad painted signs. The Lucky Cactus, the casino’s letters, the Rialto. He taught me a letter is a landscape. Mum’s a dinner lady. I paint what he taught me to see.

own.label: Ask where she draws
own.player: Where do you go to draw?
own.reply: Out the Old Mission road on my bike. I sit on an old lady’s back step without asking and draw the cracked tower. She brings me lemonade. Neither of us has ever said a word.

calls.label: Ask where the man in the cloak lives
calls.player: Do you know where the man who draws you lives?
calls.reply: I followed him home once. The flat above the old Rialto. Every window is covered in drawings of me. I saw them from the street and went home and didn’t sleep.
calls.note: Chloe Farrow followed Theon home to the flat above the old Rialto, its windows covered in drawings of her.

calls.label: Ask about her sketch of the old chapel
calls.player: What did you draw at the old chapel?
calls.reply: Thirteen figures in a circle, with candles. And something on the floor in the middle that I drew as a shadow. I don’t think it was a shadow.
calls.note: Chloe Farrow sketched thirteen figures in a candlelit circle inside the Old Mission, around something on the floor.

own.label: Ask about pastry
own.player: What’s your best thing to bake?
own.reply: Croissants. Three days of folding butter for something people eat in four bites. Love is a lot like laminated dough.

own.label: Ask about her café dream
own.player: Would you ever open your own place?
own.reply: A tiny bakery with a bell on the door and no music, just the smell. I have the name already. I won’t tell you. You’ll steal it.

own.label: Ask about wedding cakes
own.player: Do you make wedding cakes?
own.reply: Dozens. I can tell which marriages will last from how the couple taste the samples. If they share one fork, they’re fine.

own.label: Ask what the dough has taught her
own.player: What has baking taught you?
own.reply: That you can’t rush anything worth having. Bread, trust, men. Especially men.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: Is your mother a baker too?
own.reply: Josephine Mercer. She makes rings, reserved and meticulous. Dad was the baker. He left for a woman with a café when I was nine. I mean to open a better one, out of spite.

own.label: Ask about the bell on her door
own.player: Why is there a bell on your flat door?
own.reply: For practice. My bakery will have a bell and no music. I’ve been listening to that bell for years so I know exactly how it should sound.

calls.label: Ask what her tasting book shows
calls.player: What do you write down at wedding tastings?
calls.reply: The couple, the flavour, the fork. Every Bluebird wedding is in there. None of the voted-in couples shared a fork. Three of my predictions now have ribbons on their stones.
calls.note: Julia Mercer’s wedding-tasting book shows no voted-in Bluebird couple ever shared a fork, and three of those husbands are dead.

own.label: Ask about the animals
own.player: What’s it like working with animals?
own.reply: Better than people. Animals bite you honestly.

own.label: Ask about the owners
own.player: Who’s worse, the pets or the owners?
own.reply: The owners. A man brought in a ferret dressed as a pirate and asked if it was depressed. Sir, look at its hat.

own.label: Ask about the bear
own.player: Has the bear hurt any animals?
own.reply: No. But a ranger brought in a tranquilliser dart we didn’t issue. Someone’s been trying to catch that bear privately.
own.note: Rachel Lowe says someone has been privately trying to tranquillise the bear.

own.label: Ask about the hardest part of her job
own.player: What’s the hardest part of the job?
own.reply: The goodbyes. Old dogs and old men holding them. The men always say sorry to the dog. It breaks me every time.

own.label: Ask about her pets
own.player: Do you have pets of your own?
own.reply: A three-legged dog, a one-eyed cat and a tortoise nobody can date. Between them they have most of an animal.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Was your dad a vet?
own.reply: The county’s large-animal vet for thirty years. The Whitlock ranch, the lodge’s stables, everyone. Then the lodge stopped calling him and he never said why.

calls.label: Ask about the tranquilliser dart
calls.player: What do you know about that dart?
calls.reply: It’s logged in our fridge. The vet says leave it. I photographed the markings. The supplier is the same one on an invoice to the trust on the ridge. Somebody’s trying to catch that bear privately, with money that’s meant for conservation.
calls.note: Rachel Lowe says the tranquilliser dart’s supplier matches an invoice to the trust on the ridge.

calls.label: Ask why her dad stopped going to the lodge
calls.player: Why did your dad stop going to the lodge?
calls.reply: His last call-out, he came home and said there was a horse with a man’s saddle on it that hadn’t been ridden in a year, and a stall at the end with a chain on the door. He never went back. They got a vet from the city.
calls.note: Rachel Lowe’s father saw a chained stall and an unridden horse with a man’s saddle at the lodge’s stables.

own.label: Ask about her job
own.player: Is it weird looking in people’s mouths all day?
own.reply: You learn everything about a person from their teeth. Coffee, wine, grinding. Grinding means they’re hiding something.

own.label: Ask about her first love
own.player: Who was your first love?
own.reply: A boy who wrote me a poem that rhymed Megan with vegan. I married him in my head for three years.

own.label: Ask who grinds their teeth
own.player: Who in Sunfall grinds their teeth the worst?
own.reply: Can’t say names. But a certain foundation treasurer has cracked two crowns since the gala.
own.note: Megan O’Keefe says the foundation treasurer has cracked two crowns grinding his teeth since the gala.

own.label: Ask what a smile tells her
own.player: What does someone’s smile tell you?
own.reply: Everything. Whether they’re nervous, whether they’re lying, whether they had coffee. Yours looks honest, for what it’s worth.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Were your family dentists?
own.reply: Pub people. Dad ran a bar, sold it, and became a dental technician. I followed him. Mum reads the same romances I do. We swap them.

own.label: Ask about working for the mayor
own.player: What’s it like working for the mayor?
own.reply: He’s a dentist. He talks in the chair about the planning committee because I’m the hygienist and don’t count. I write it in my scrapbook between the poems.

calls.label: Ask about the charts she keeps
calls.player: What do your patients’ charts tell you lately?
calls.reply: The treasurer has cracked two crowns. The events director had a tooth replaced, knocked out, he says, by a car door. Car doors don’t usually swing that hard.
calls.note: Megan O’Keefe says Augustus Pell has cracked two crowns and Dorian Kell had a tooth knocked out after the gala.

calls.label: Ask what the mayor talks about
calls.player: What does the mayor talk about in the chair?
calls.reply: Canal side. Variance. The Sisters. In that order, every time. I don’t know what a variance is, but I know it’s about the Sisters’ land.
calls.note: Megan O’Keefe says the mayor keeps talking about a canal-side planning variance and the Sisters’ land.

own.label: Ask what she studies
own.player: What are you studying?
own.reply: History. I like the dead. They don’t text back, but they don’t ghost you either.

own.label: Ask about campus life
own.player: Is campus as tense as everyone says?
own.reply: You can’t say anything in seminars. I write what I actually think in my notebook and say something safe out loud.

own.label: Ask what she’s scared of
own.player: What scares you about leaving college?
own.reply: That I’ll get a job I hate, a flat I can’t afford, and nobody to come home to. Everyone says you have time. Do I?

own.label: Ask what she’ll do after college
own.player: What happens after college?
own.reply: Everyone keeps asking. I have a degree in a subject I picked at eighteen and a debt I can’t picture. I’ll probably be fine. Probably.

own.label: Ask how she’s a senior at eighteen
own.player: How are you in your final year at eighteen?
own.reply: I started at sixteen on the early-entry scheme and I’ve been overlooked ever since. Being young in a seminar is like being furniture with opinions.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Who are your family?
own.reply: Dad’s a librarian at the university. Mum left for the coast when I was twelve and writes, sometimes. I learned to be quiet in libraries and it stuck everywhere else.

calls.label: Ask about her dissertation
calls.player: What’s your dissertation about?
calls.reply: The thirtieth year. The year the parish moved the founding families’ weddings from the Old Mission to St Brigid’s, the year the bell cracked, and the year the sewing circle became a charity. Three changes in one year. Nobody writes about why.
calls.note: Emma Frost says the founding families stopped marrying at the Old Mission in the same year its bell cracked and the sewing circle became the charity.

own.label: Ask about the cinema
own.player: What’s it like working at the cinema?
own.reply: Free popcorn and watching the ends of films I’ve never seen the start of. I know how everything ends and nothing about how it began.

own.label: Ask about films now
own.player: Are films worse now?
own.reply: Everything is a sequel, a remake or a superhero. Nobody takes a risk any more. I miss films that trusted you to be sad.

own.label: Ask about a regular customer
own.player: Any strange regulars?
own.reply: A man buys a ticket to the late showing every night and never watches the film. He sits in the lobby facing the car park.

own.label: Ask which film ending she’d change
own.player: Which film ending would you change?
own.reply: None. Sad endings are the honest ones. Real life doesn’t do credits.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: Brown Avenue. Dad runs a garage, my brother’s a mechanic, my sister’s still at school. Our kitchen smells of engine oil and toast.

own.label: Ask why her dad lost the Foundation
own.player: Did your dad ever lose a big customer?
own.reply: The Foundation took its cars to a garage on the ridge road instead. Dad said once that their cars came back with things in the boot he didn’t want to see. Then he changed the subject to carburettors.

calls.label: Ask what the man in the lobby is doing
calls.player: What’s the man in the lobby doing every night?
calls.reply: His name’s Ken Yamada. He built the lodge’s cellar. He sits facing the car park because the lodge’s van parks there for the all-night pharmacy, and he counts the men. He told me on the third coffee.
calls.note: Paige Dalton says Ken Yamada, who built the lodge’s cellar, sits in the cinema lobby counting the men from the lodge’s van.

own.label: Ask about planning events
own.player: What’s the worst event you’ve planned?
own.reply: A gender reveal where the cannon set fire to a hedge. The baby’s fine. The hedge is not.

own.label: Ask about the wedding industry
own.player: Are weddings out of control?
own.reply: Couples spend a year’s salary on one day and then can’t afford the marriage. I tell them: spend less on the flowers, more on the counselling.

own.label: Ask about the gala set-up
own.player: Did you work on the gala?
own.reply: I set up the tables. Table 9 was moved twice on the day, closer to the kitchen. Nobody would tell me why.
own.note: Nicole Ashbury says Table 9 was moved closer to the kitchen twice on gala day.

own.label: Ask what her own wedding would be like
own.player: What would your own wedding be like?
own.reply: Small. A church, a dress that fits, and nobody filming. I’ve planned two hundred weddings for other people and every one of them was for the camera.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are you married?
own.reply: To a sound engineer at the Vestry. Two children who think the benefit is where Mummy goes to shout at florists. They’re not wrong.

own.label: Ask how she got into events
own.player: How did you get into events?
own.reply: Mum ran the late-service crew at the club for years. I grew up stacking chairs with the volunteers at midnight. Mum still knows every waitress in Sunfall by name.

calls.label: Ask about the day’s seating plan
calls.player: Do you still have the real seating plan?
calls.reply: Not the published one. The day’s, with the two moves of Table 9 in my handwriting and the times, and the man who told me to do it: Dorian Kell. The volunteer who asked me why was wearing a badge that said Elena.
calls.note: Nicole Ashbury’s seating plan shows Dorian Kell ordered Table 9 moved, and the volunteer who asked why wore a badge saying Elena.

calls.label: Ask if her mother knows the catering crew
calls.player: Does your mum know the late-service crew?
calls.reply: Every one. She knows who R.M. is: Ruth Marchetti. And she knows where Ruth went. She says she’ll tell nobody. She told me.
calls.note: Nicole Ashbury says R.M. is Ruth Marchetti of the late-service crew, and her mother knows where Ruth went.

own.label: Ask about the rodeo
own.player: What’s the rodeo like?
own.reply: Dust, beer and men who think they can ride a bull. Some of them can. Most of them are brave in a way that’s mostly stupid.

own.label: Ask if she rides
own.player: Do you ride?
own.reply: Since I was four. Horses are honest. They know if you’re scared before you do.

own.label: Ask about real cowboys
own.player: Are there real cowboys left?
own.reply: A few. They don’t own phones and they hold doors. My grandpa was one. I’m still waiting for one my age.

own.label: Ask about her worst fall
own.player: What was your worst fall?
own.reply: Broke my wrist at sixteen. Got back on the next season. My dad said the horse doesn’t care about your feelings, and he was right.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A room at the Whitlock ranch. I work the horses with Isabel and ride the canyon road. I tell the collision lady which days the grey car is on it.

own.label: Ask about her grandfather
own.player: Who’s the old cowboy?
own.reply: My grandpa Buck. Real cowboy, no teeth, laughs like a door. He rode with Diana Moore’s first husband and was in the arena the day the bull killed him.

calls.label: Ask what her grandfather says about the bull
calls.player: What does your grandpa say about that day?
calls.reply: That the bull wasn’t the bull Tommy drew. It was swapped in the chute by the stock contractor, whose business the casino bought the next year. And Tommy’s widow was taken to lunch at the funeral by a lady from the club.
calls.note: Audrey King’s grandfather says the bull that killed Tommy Moore was swapped in the chute.

own.label: Ask about the library
own.player: What’s the library like?
own.reply: Quiet, cool, and full of the only people in Sunfall who still read for pleasure. We’re a secret society with late fees.

own.label: Ask about banned books
own.player: Do people try to ban books?
own.reply: From both sides! One group wants to ban the old novels, another wants to ban the new ones. I keep both and hide the complaints in the returns box.

own.label: Ask what’s been borrowed
own.player: Has anyone borrowed anything strange?
own.reply: Someone’s taken out every book we have on moon cycles and old Latin rites. Always the same library card. It belongs to a man who died last year.
own.note: Someone is borrowing every library book on moon cycles and Latin rites on a dead man’s card.

own.label: Ask why libraries matter
own.player: Why do libraries still matter?
own.reply: Because they’re the last place in town where you can sit for free and nobody tries to sell you anything. That’s rarer than gold now.

own.label: Ask about her sisters
own.player: Are you close to your sisters?
own.reply: Odette does the radio, Samantha sells houses, I keep the library. Once a week we meet here and argue. I run the quietest room in Sunfall and I’m the loudest person in it.

own.label: Ask what the library is really for
own.player: What is a library really for?
own.reply: A secret society with late fees. The last place in town you can sit for free and nobody sells you anything. Both sides have tried to ban things. I lend them all.

calls.label: Ask about the books on the dead man’s card
calls.player: Who borrows the books on moon cycles?
calls.reply: Every one, on the same card. Harold Oakley’s. He died last year. His grandson Ethan uses it. Moon cycles, Latin rites, the old mission. I lend them, because I lend everything. But I’ve started writing the dates down.
calls.note: Bethany Price says Ethan Oakley borrows books on moon cycles and Latin rites on his late grandfather’s library card.

own.label: Ask about lifeguarding
own.player: Is lifeguarding as easy as it looks?
own.reply: It’s eight hours of watching people almost drown and then not. I’ve saved four children and one very proud businessman.

own.label: Ask about influencers at the pool
own.player: Do influencers come to the pool?
own.reply: Every day. They film themselves living their best life for forty minutes and never touch the water.

own.label: Ask about night swimmers
own.player: Does anyone swim at night?
own.reply: The club pool. On the gala night someone threw a phone in the deep end. I fished it out the next morning. It’s in the lost property box. Nobody’s claimed it.
own.note: Erin Doyle found a phone thrown in the club pool on gala night; it’s unclaimed in lost property.

own.label: Ask about the one she saved
own.player: Have you ever actually saved someone?
own.reply: A little boy, my first summer. His mum was filming a video for her followers. She never thanked me. She posted the video.

own.label: Ask if she’s a member of the club
own.player: Are you a member at the club?
own.reply: Staff, not a member. I say it before anyone else can. Mum cleans there, which is how I got the pool. It’s the only thing at the club I have that she cleans.

own.label: Ask who she lives with
own.player: Do you live alone?
own.reply: With Georgina, who coaches swimming. We swam county together. I beat her on the shout and she’s never let it go. We get on brilliantly.

calls.label: Ask what was on the phone from the pool
calls.player: Did you ever turn that phone on?
calls.reply: I did. The lock screen is a blue dress on a hanger, next to a notebook. It’s Elena Cross’s, or it was. It’s locked, and it’s in the lost-property box in the plant room. Someone else has the key.
calls.note: Erin Doyle says the phone fished out of the club pool is Elena Cross’s, kept in the plant room’s lost property.

calls.label: Ask about the boy she saved
calls.player: Who was the little boy you saved?
calls.reply: Celeste Van Doren’s grandson. His mum’s the influencer who filmed it. The video has a hundred thousand views and my face in it, and since then the club has asked me to be discreet about the pool.

own.label: Ask about office life
own.player: What’s office life like?
own.reply: Endless meetings about meetings. I run the place and nobody knows it. Without me the coffee machine and the printer would both have died years ago.

own.label: Ask what she does to escape
own.player: What do you do to escape?
own.reply: Motorbike, desert roads, no helmet camera. If I fall off, at least it won’t be online.

own.label: Ask about working from home
own.player: Do you ever wish you worked from home?
own.reply: Never. My friends who work from home talk to their cats more than people. An office is annoying. Loneliness is worse.

own.label: Ask what she’d do if she quit
own.player: What would you do if you quit tomorrow?
own.reply: Drive to the coast and open a bait shop. I’ve never fished. I just want a job where nobody sends me a calendar invite.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are you one of the Lucky Cactus Brookses?
own.reply: Dolores’s third girl, Christina’s twin. Four sisters running a diner in shifts and fighting about the booth. I do the weekday accounts. Nobody else can add.

own.label: Ask about her motorbike
own.player: Where do you ride?
own.reply: Desert roads, no helmet camera. If I fall off, at least it won’t be online. Out past the canyon the road’s so straight you can hear yourself think.

calls.label: Ask about the planning files she copied
calls.player: What’s in the planning files?
calls.reply: Three files. A canal-side variance for the diocese and a consultancy on the ridge. The ridge road leased to a trust. And the weigh station at the junction: the county owns it, the trust rents it. The mayor’s signature is on all three. I copied them on the printer I keep alive.
calls.note: Kimberly Brooks copied planning files showing the mayor signed the trust’s ridge-road lease and its lease of the weigh station.

calls.label: Ask about the circles in the office diary
calls.player: Why do you draw circles in the office diary?
calls.reply: The mayor’s committee only ever meets on nights with no moon. I started drawing a little circle in the margin each time. The next one’s {night}.

own.label: Ask about the ice-cream van
own.player: What’s it like driving an ice-cream van?
own.reply: Everyone’s happy to see you. It’s the only job where that’s true. Except the dentists. They glare.

own.label: Ask her favourite flavour
own.player: What’s your favourite flavour?
own.reply: Prickly pear sorbet. It tastes like Sunfall: sweet, pink and slightly dangerous.

own.label: Ask what she sees on her route
own.player: Do you see much driving around all day?
own.reply: A grey car follows the same route as me some days, slowly, like it’s looking for someone. It doesn’t buy ice cream. People who don’t buy ice cream are suspicious.
own.note: Grace Wheeler sees a grey car slowly driving her ice-cream route, as if looking for someone.

own.label: Ask what kids teach her
own.player: What do the kids on your route teach you?
own.reply: That joy is cheap. Two dollars and a cone. The grown-ups queue with their phones out and never look up.

own.label: Ask who had the van before her
own.player: Did someone run the van before you?
own.reply: My grandma, forty years. She sold ice cream to the club children at the gate and was never once let in. She kept a route book of every stop. I inherited it with the chime.

own.label: Ask what the van is called
own.player: Does the van have a name?
own.reply: Dolores, like the jukebox, because the Brooks girls let me park at the Lucky Cactus. It plays one tune and breaks down on hills. It’s perfect.

calls.label: Ask about her grandmother’s route book
calls.player: What’s in your grandma’s route book?
calls.reply: Forty years of stops, and the names of the club children. By the stop at the Cemetery Chapel she wrote: the ribbon children. Two scoops. Never charged. I don’t understand it. I think she did.
calls.note: Grace Wheeler’s grandmother’s route book calls the children by the Cemetery Chapel the ribbon children, never charged.

calls.label: Ask about the grey car
calls.player: Did you ever get the grey car’s number?
calls.reply: I wrote the plate on a cone wrapper and gave it to a policewoman from the archive. Kelsey. She thanked me and put it in her pocket. I haven’t heard anything since.
calls.note: Grace Wheeler gave the grey car’s number plate to Kelsey Donovan, and heard nothing more.

own.label: Ask about training horses
own.player: How do you train a horse?
own.reply: Patience. You can’t force trust, only earn it. People could learn a lot from horses.

own.label: Ask about the ranch
own.player: Where do you work?
own.reply: A ranch out past the canyon, owned by a family that’s been here five generations. The developers keep offering. The old man keeps saying no.

own.label: Ask about family
own.player: Do you want a family?
own.reply: A big one. Kids, horses, a long table, too much noise. My friends think that’s quaint. I think it’s the whole point.

own.label: Ask how a horse learns to trust
own.player: How does a horse learn to trust you?
own.reply: Slowly, and only if you’re the same every day. Horses can’t be flattered. Neither can I.

own.label: Ask about the ranch house
own.player: What’s it like living at the ranch?
own.reply: A long table with too much noise. The old man, his grandson Jesse, Audrey from the rodeo and me. Every dinner is an argument about horses and land and who left the gate open.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: What was your mum like?
own.reply: She died when I was seventeen, of a thing they caught late. Inez got her politics from that. I got my patience. Same grief, different directions.

calls.label: Ask if anyone at the ranch is in trouble
calls.player: Is anyone at the ranch in trouble?
calls.reply: Jesse, the old man’s grandson. He was in love with Alice Beaumont and wasn’t approved. Now he rides the fastest horse up the ridge road at night, alone, and comes back before dawn. I haven’t told his grandfather.
calls.note: Isabel Morales says Jesse Whitlock rides up the ridge road alone at night since the club refused him.

own.label: Ask about the flower shop
own.player: What’s it like running a flower shop?
own.reply: Quiet, mostly. People only buy flowers when something big happens: love, death, apology. I see the whole town’s heart.

own.label: Ask about the meaning of flowers
own.player: Do flowers still mean things?
own.reply: They used to. Red roses for love, yellow for friendship. Now people just want whatever photographs well.

own.label: Ask about a strange order
own.player: Have you had any strange orders?
own.reply: White lilies, every few days, delivered to the old interstate junction. No card. Paid in cash. Lilies are for funerals.
own.note: Elena Vargas delivers white lilies to the old interstate junction every few days, paid in cash, no card.

own.label: Ask which flower lasts longest
own.player: Which flower lasts the longest?
own.reply: Chrysanthemums. People think they’re funeral flowers. They are. They’re also the ones still standing when the roses have gone.

own.label: Ask about her flower dictionaries
own.player: Do flowers really mean things?
own.reply: I’ve a shelf of flower dictionaries. Red for love, yellow for friendship. Now people just want whatever photographs well. The flowers still mean it, even if nobody reads them.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Did your family grow flowers?
own.reply: Dad kept the Bluebird Club’s grounds for twenty years, until the lodge’s men took over the planting. He said once they planted lilies at the Cemetery Chapel on the club’s instructions. He doesn’t garden any more.

calls.label: Ask who sends the lilies
calls.player: Who sends the lilies to the junction?
calls.reply: The cash comes through my door in an envelope with no name. Twice I’ve seen the woman who posts it: tall, a creased white linen suit, sleepy eyes. She waits until it’s through, then walks to the reservoir side. A widow, I think. I don’t know whose.
calls.note: Elena Vargas says the lilies for the old junction are paid for by a tall widow in a white linen suit from the reservoir side.

own.label: Ask about cosmetology
own.player: What’s cosmetology school like?
own.reply: Doing eyebrows on mannequins called Brenda. I’ve made Brenda beautiful forty times. She never thanks me.

own.label: Ask about everyone looking the same
own.player: Why does everyone online have the same face?
own.reply: Same filters, same fillers, same three tutorials. I want to teach women to look like themselves, just more.

own.label: Ask about her love life
own.player: Are you a romantic?
own.reply: Completely. I want flowers, a slow dance and someone who looks at me like I’m the only person in the room. Apparently that’s a lot.

own.label: Ask what she thinks is beautiful
own.player: What do you think is actually beautiful?
own.reply: Faces that look like someone. Everyone at school wants the same face from the same filter. My nan’s face had eighty years in it. That was beautiful.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you have a twin?
own.reply: Imogen. She’s loud where I’m soft. She works at the radio and paints Brown Avenue. Our big sister Catalina is the brave one, at the club. We all three look the same and nothing alike.

own.label: Ask about the photo above her mirror
own.player: Whose photo is above your mirror?
own.reply: My nan. She raised us. Her face had eighty years in it. When I do someone’s make-up I think: let them look like that, one day.

calls.label: Ask if she’s seen anything odd on Hinge
calls.player: Seen anything odd on the app?
calls.reply: A profile with your name under it and your pictures. Except one, where the eyes are wrong. I know those eyes. I did that face for a student show at seventeen. A boy called Theon. Someone’s wearing you.
calls.note: Camila Reyes recognised Theon’s eyes in a Hinge profile that uses your name and pictures.

calls.label: Ask about her sister’s photograph
calls.player: What happened with your sister’s photograph?
calls.reply: I did Catalina’s face for the club’s picture. Now that photo is on an invitation to a private dinner, sent to a girl on Brown Avenue in Catalina’s name. My work, on a thing that frightens me.
calls.note: Camila Reyes says her sister Catalina’s club photograph is being used on private dinner invitations sent in Catalina’s name.

own.label: Ask about being a ranger
own.player: What’s a park ranger’s day like?
own.reply: Telling tourists not to touch cacti, and then pulling cactus out of tourists.

own.label: Ask about the bear
own.player: What’s the real story with the bear?
own.reply: He’s a young male, pushed out by an older one. He’s lost, hungry and too curious. Honestly? Relatable.

own.label: Ask about the bear’s collar
own.player: Is it true the bear has a collar?
own.reply: It does. It isn’t ours. Someone tagged him without telling the park service, and the signal goes to a private receiver.
own.note: Marisol Fuentes says the bear wears a tracking collar that isn’t the park’s, sending to a private receiver.

own.label: Ask about the night sky out there
own.player: What’s the night sky like out in the desert?
own.reply: Like being told how small you are, kindly. Everyone should get told that once a week.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A ranger’s cabin at the end of the canyon, with a telescope I never use and a dog I always do. My parents were rangers too. Mum was the county’s first woman ranger.

own.label: Ask about her parents
own.player: Where are your parents now?
own.reply: Retired to a house halfway up the ridge road. Mum sits on the porch and watches the vans go up to the lodge. She says it’s better than television.

calls.label: Ask where the collar’s signal goes
calls.player: Where does the bear’s collar signal go?
calls.reply: I tracked it on my own time with the service’s receiver. It’s strongest at the lodge gate. My director, who dines at the lodge, told me to leave it. I haven’t.
calls.note: Marisol Fuentes tracked the bear’s collar signal to the lodge gate.

calls.label: Ask about the illegal trap
calls.player: Who set the trap the rangers didn’t?
calls.reply: I have the trap’s manufacturer plate. It was bought on the Foundation’s conservation grant. Somebody is using conservation money to catch a bear for a lodge.
calls.note: Marisol Fuentes says the illegal bear trap was bought with the Foundation’s conservation grant.

own.label: Ask about her boutique
own.player: What do you sell?
own.reply: Dresses for women who want to feel like the main character for one evening. Then they go home and take their shoes off in the car.

own.label: Ask about fast fashion
own.player: Can a boutique survive fast fashion?
own.reply: Barely. People buy ten dresses that fall apart instead of one that lasts. I sell the one that lasts.

own.label: Ask about a dress she sold
own.player: Do you remember a dress you sold?
own.reply: I sold Elena Cross her blue gala dress. She asked for one with pockets deep enough for a phone and a notebook. Who takes a notebook to a party?
own.note: Daniela Cruz sold Elena Cross a blue gala dress with pockets deep enough for a phone and a notebook.

own.label: Ask what makes something well made
own.player: What makes something well made?
own.reply: Seams you never notice, and a fabric that gets better with age. Like people, honestly. The ones worth keeping improve.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Is Hector your dad?
own.reply: Hector and his taco van, yes. Mum died when Paola and I were twelve and he bought a van and fed the town. I have lunch with him every day. Free tacos are the best inheritance.

own.label: Ask about her neighbour
own.player: Who’s next door to the boutique?
own.reply: The jeweller. I can see straight into her window from my sewing room. She sells to the club. She also sells to people who arrive after dark.

calls.label: Ask about the gowns for private dinners
calls.player: What do the club girls order from you?
calls.reply: Gowns for private dinners. The juniors order them without knowing what for, and they’re all the same dress: pale, a sheath, like a slip. The one Valerie Huxley wears in her portrait. Every time.
calls.note: Daniela Cruz says every gown ordered for the club’s private dinners is the same pale dress.

own.label: Ask about design work
own.player: What do you design?
own.reply: Logos for companies that don’t exist yet and won’t exist next year. Currently: a disruptive sandwich app.

own.label: Ask why everything looks the same
own.player: Why do all brands look the same now?
own.reply: Everyone copied the same three tech companies: flat, beige, rounded, friendly. It’s the visual equivalent of saying nothing politely.

own.label: Ask about a strange commission
own.player: Have you had a strange commission?
own.reply: Someone paid me to design a crescent symbol for an exclusive social club. No name, cash. I recognised it later on a gig poster.
own.note: Hana Park designed a crescent symbol for an anonymous exclusive social club, later seen on a gig poster.

own.label: Ask what she’d make if nobody paid her
own.player: What would you make if nobody was paying you?
own.reply: Something ugly and alive. Every client wants clean and minimal. Clean and minimal is what a hospital looks like.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What did your family do?
own.reply: We had a dry cleaner’s that closed when I was thirteen. Dad went to the city. Mum went quiet. I became the artist and my sister became the earner.

own.label: Ask where she works
own.player: Where do you work?
own.reply: A flat above the dance studio. I can hear ballroom lessons through the floor. My logos all have a waltz in them now, very faintly.

calls.label: Ask about the crescent commission
calls.player: Who commissioned the crescent?
calls.reply: Three lines and a sketch, in a hand I now know from the club’s Christmas cards, and the cash came in an envelope with the Foundation’s watermark on the flap. I’ve hidden the brief in the back of a picture frame, because my sister visits.
calls.note: Hana Park says the crescent commission came in the club’s Christmas-card handwriting, paid in a Foundation envelope.

own.label: Ask about the salon
own.player: What’s it like doing hair?
own.reply: People tell their hairdresser everything. I’m quieter than most, so they tell me even more.

own.label: Ask what people confess
own.player: What do people confess in the chair?
own.reply: Affairs, debts, crushes. A woman once told me she’d never loved her husband. Then she tipped me forty dollars and went home to him.

own.label: Ask about a client
own.player: Has a client said anything worrying?
own.reply: A woman from the foundation had me dye her hair dark the morning after the gala. Very dark. She said she needed to look different for a while.
own.note: Mei Chen dyed a foundation woman’s hair very dark the morning after the gala because she needed to look different.

own.label: Ask what people say in the chair
own.player: What do people tell you in the chair?
own.reply: Everything they can’t tell their husbands. I’ve heard three affairs and one confession of murder. The murder was a cat. Still.

own.label: Ask how she became a hairdresser
own.player: How did you get into hair?
own.reply: A course at sixteen, the only one we could afford. I turned out to be good at the listening part. The cutting came later.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Who lives upstairs?
own.reply: My sister Daisy. I hear everything and say nothing. She makes art and says nothing. The street thinks we’re a comedy double act.

calls.label: Ask about the murder confession
calls.player: Who confessed to the cat?
calls.reply: A grand lady from the club. Honoria Blackwood. The cat was the mother of her daughter’s cat, and she said it was the last time she’d clean up after her daughter. Then she tipped me very well.
calls.note: Mei Chen says Honoria Blackwood confessed to killing her estranged daughter’s cat’s mother.

own.label: Ask about community theatre
own.player: What are you rehearsing?
own.reply: A musical about the founding of Sunfall. I play a pioneer woman who dies of fever in act one. I die beautifully.

own.label: Ask why she acts
own.player: Why do you love acting?
own.reply: Because for two hours, everyone in the room agrees to feel the same thing. That hardly ever happens any more.

own.label: Ask about the director
own.player: What’s your director like?
own.reply: He cast me for diversity and said so out loud. I wanted the part because I’m good. Both of those things can be true, and only one was his business.

own.label: Ask which role she’d die to play
own.player: Which role would you give anything to play?
own.reply: Lady Macbeth. Everyone wants to play the nice girl. The nice girl never gets the speech.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Do your family come to your shows?
own.reply: Every one. Dad drives buses and Mum nurses nights. They sit in the front row and Mum cries when I die in act one, every time, even though she knows.

own.label: Ask what she wants from acting
own.player: What do you want from acting?
own.reply: Somewhere to belong. A company that’s mine. The Players are lovely, but they’re a Foundation production, and it shows in the songs.

calls.label: Ask about the boy who spoke in verse
calls.player: Who was the boy who spoke in verse?
calls.reply: Theon. We did a student play together, three years ago, before they sent him down. I was the only one who was kind to him. He still sends me a line on my birthday.
calls.note: Nia Walker was in a student play with Theon before he was sent down.

calls.label: Ask when the musical opens
calls.player: When does the founding musical open?
calls.reply: {night}, the night with no moon, which is a strange choice for a show about pioneers. Act two has nine women singing a round at the Old Mission. Somebody copied the music from the club’s archive.

own.label: Ask about planning the gala
own.player: How’s the gala planning going?
own.reply: Three hundred guests, one string quartet and a seating plan that would make a general weep. I adore it.

own.label: Ask about Professor Vale
own.player: You’re friends with Professor Vale?
own.reply: Adrian is the most delightful man in Sunfall. He says the unsayable over dessert. We need more men brave enough to be disliked.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do for fun, away from the galas?
own.reply: I ride. Horses don’t care who your father was, which is refreshing.

own.label: Ask what she really wants
own.player: What do you really want, Alice?
own.reply: To run the Foundation one day, and to run it honestly. That second part is harder than people think.

own.label: Ask about the portrait in her hall
own.player: Who’s in the big portrait in your hall?
own.reply: Ada Beaumont, my great-grandmother. Founding family. Look closely at her brooch next time anyone lets you in: there’s a crescent in it. I asked my father why once. He changed the subject so fast he nearly fell over it.

own.label: Ask how she spends money
own.player: Do you think about money much?
own.reply: Not at all, which is the luxury. I spend it like weather. But I know to the penny what everybody else at the club spends, and on whom. That’s not money. That’s maps.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you get on with your sister?
own.reply: Audra was meant to be the heir and stepped aside for me. She wears dead women’s dresses to dinners to make a point. I love her. I have never understood the point.

views.campus: If you can’t bear to hear an idea, you haven’t got an education, you’ve got a fan club.
views.speakers: Paglia was a triumph and Houellebecq was a delight. The Progressives call them dangerous. Ideas are only dangerous to people who haven’t got any.
views.thunderbirds: We fund half the good in this town and get blamed for the other half.

calls.label: Ask who she trusts at the club
calls.player: Who do you actually trust at the club?
calls.reply: I keep two lists in my head. Everyone who’ll be loyal to me when Honoria is gone. And a much shorter one: the women who sit at the treasurer’s table. I haven’t decided yet whether to burn that table or inherit it.
calls.note: Alice Beaumont says there is an inner circle at the treasurer’s table, and she hasn’t decided whether to break it or take it over.

calls.label: Ask what the founders were really like
calls.player: What were the founding women really like?
calls.reply: Before the charity, before the club, they used to sit up at the Old Mission on nights with no moon. Ada’s letters say so. Grandmother called it their little religion. Nobody at the club says the word mission without looking at the floor.
calls.note: Alice Beaumont says the founding Bluebird women once met at the Old Mission on moonless nights.

own.label: Ask what drives her
own.player: What gets you out of bed in the morning?
own.reply: Winning. Targets, tennis, auctions. I don’t do taking part. Taking part is what losers call it.

own.label: Ask about women in charge
own.player: Is it hard being a woman running things here?
own.reply: Not really. The men are scared of me and the women want my diary. The real problem is everyone younger wants a title before they’ve done the work.

own.label: Ask about Dorian Kell
own.player: What do you make of Dorian Kell?
own.reply: Charming, connected, and he never once looks you in the eye when he talks about money. I keep my handbag closed around Dorian.
own.note: Caroline Prescott doesn’t trust Dorian Kell around money.

own.label: Ask if ambition is lonely
own.player: Is ambition lonely?
own.reply: Very. Men tell me I’m intimidating like it’s a diagnosis. I’d trade three board seats for one man who wasn’t threatened by them.

own.label: Ask where she keeps her trophies
own.player: Where do you keep all the trophies?
own.reply: In the downstairs loo. People have to sit and look at them. It’s the only time anyone at the club stays still long enough to be impressed.

own.label: Ask who she plays tennis with
own.player: Who do you play tennis with?
own.reply: I have a court in my garden and nobody to play on it. The good ones are scared of losing and the bad ones are scared of me. I hit against the wall. The wall is a gentleman.

own.label: Ask about the Prescotts
own.player: Your family built something here, didn’t they?
own.reply: The dam’s second wall. We lost a son on it, my great-uncle, nineteen. There’s a plaque. Everyone reads the plaque and nobody reads the name.

own.label: Ask about the man who left
own.player: Has anyone ever left you?
own.reply: Daniel. He left the month after a man from the club bought him lunch. I thought he’d stopped loving me. I’ve since worked out he hadn’t. He left so they couldn’t use him. That’s worse.

calls.label: Ask what she’s working on in secret
calls.player: You sound like someone working on something in secret.
calls.reply: Nine years of donor records, the dates a certain events director signed anything, and every payment to a trust on the ridge. I could end something with it. The trouble is, the real work dies with the fraud, and my own mother is in one of the photographs.
calls.note: Caroline Prescott keeps a private file on nine years of payments to the trust on the ridge.

calls.label: Ask about her mother
calls.player: Is your mother still at the club?
calls.reply: She’s at the lodge on Halcyon Ridge more than she’s at home. I have a photograph of her up there with a man who never appears on any guest list. Lyle Marchbanks. Remember the name and then forget I said it.
calls.note: Caroline Prescott says a man called Lyle Marchbanks is often at the lodge and never on any guest list.

own.label: Ask about the volunteers
own.player: Who actually volunteers at these things?
own.reply: Retirees, students who need it for their CV, and the Sisters, who do the real work and never post about it.

own.label: Ask what keeps her sane
own.player: How do you stay sane doing that job?
own.reply: I run the canyon trail before sunrise. No phone. It’s the only hour of the day nobody needs anything from me.

own.label: Ask about the gala rota
own.player: Were you working the night of the gala?
own.reply: I did the rota. Two volunteers were swapped off Table 9 at the last minute and replaced by people I’d never met. The order came from upstairs.
own.note: Phoebe Sutton says two volunteers were swapped off Table 9 at the last minute on orders from upstairs.

own.label: Ask what nobody notices about her work
own.player: What does nobody notice about your work?
own.reply: The chairs. Somebody has to put out four hundred chairs and stack them again at midnight. It’s always the same five women.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you live alone?
own.reply: With my little sister, Molly, who talks enough for both of us. I cook, pay the bills and am asleep by ten. She answers the phone at the Foundation and names cacti.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: How did your family end up at the club?
own.reply: We had the boat yard on the reservoir until the club bought it for the sailing annex. That’s how a working family gets two daughters in: as staff who are allowed to call themselves members. Dad drinks on the boats he used to own.

own.label: Ask who stacks the chairs
own.player: Who actually does the work at those nights?
own.reply: The same five women stack four hundred chairs at midnight. I’m one. Three are Sisters of Mercy. They never post about it. The board posts about it.

own.label: Ask what her volunteers found
own.player: Did your volunteers find anything when they cleared up?
own.reply: One of my five found a torn ticket under the treasurer’s table and handed it to the Sisters’ lost property, because she trusts nuns more than the committee. So do I. I’ll ask her to send you a photograph of it.

calls.label: Ask about the original rota
calls.player: Do you still have the rota from before it was changed?
calls.reply: I kept it. The order to swap two of my volunteers off Table 9 came from upstairs, meaning the events director’s office. The men who replaced them wore our lanyards and didn’t stack a single chair. My sister answers the phone in that office. That’s why I’ve said nothing.
calls.note: Phoebe Sutton kept the original rota; the order to swap Table 9’s volunteers came from the events director’s office.

own.label: Ask what a community liaison does
own.player: What does a community liaison do?
own.reply: I translate. Rich people say outreach and poor people say rent. I stand in the middle and make sure nobody gets slapped.

own.label: Ask if she sets people up
own.player: Do you ever set people up?
own.reply: Constantly. Three marriages and a very messy divorce. I’ve already decided which of my friends you’d suit. Don’t ask. Fine, ask.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: My abuela crossed a desert to get here and now I organise canapés for people whose grandfathers owned the desert. She thinks it’s hilarious. So do I, most days.

own.label: Ask who she’d set you up with
own.player: Who would you set me up with, if not you?
own.reply: Nobody, now. I’m keeping you. That’s the risk of being a matchmaker: sometimes you meet the good one first.

own.label: Ask about her grandmother
own.player: Tell me about your abuela.
own.reply: She crossed a desert to get here. Now I serve canapés to the grandsons of the men who owned it. We both think it’s hilarious. Most days.

own.label: Ask about the shortbread war
own.player: Is it true about your mum’s shortbread?
own.reply: Better than Sophia Moretti’s, whatever the parish says. The Sisters judge it every bake sale and it’s always a draw, which is how nuns say no.

own.label: Ask what her job really is
own.player: What do you actually spend your days doing?
own.reply: The food programme, the scholarship interviews, the parish partnerships. Three jobs, one salary. I stand between people who say outreach and people who say rent, and nobody gets slapped.

calls.label: Ask about her father
calls.player: What happened to your dad?
calls.reply: He drove deliveries for the Foundation. After he died I found his last sheet in his jacket. One drop at the old junction, for the Halcyon Ridge Trust. Crates, not food. I’ve kept it nine years. I matchmake instead of opening that drawer.
calls.note: Sofia Delgado kept her late father’s delivery sheet: crates for the Halcyon Ridge Trust, dropped at the old junction.

calls.label: Ask what the Sisters are up to
calls.player: Anything odd going on at the chapel?
calls.reply: My mum bakes for the Sisters. She counts plates the way other people count money. There’s one more plate going up the back stairs of the charity shop than there are Sisters. Every day. I didn’t say that.
calls.note: Sofia Delgado says an extra plate of food goes up the back stairs of the Sisters’ charity shop every day.

own.label: Ask about keeping the books
own.player: Is accounting for a charity as dull as it sounds?
own.reply: Duller. Except when it isn’t. Charity accounts are where the most interesting lies in town are written down in very neat columns.

own.label: Ask about her style
own.player: You always look immaculate. Is that on purpose?
own.reply: Everything is on purpose. If you look perfect, people assume you’re perfect, and they stop checking your work. Useful, for an accountant.

own.label: Ask what she’s noticed
own.player: Have you noticed anything odd in the accounts?
own.reply: Someone pays a catering firm that doesn’t cater. Same amount, every quarter. I’ve flagged it twice. The flags keep disappearing.
own.note: Yumi Tanaka says the foundation pays a catering firm that doesn’t cater, and her flags keep disappearing.

own.label: Ask what numbers tell her about people
own.player: What do the numbers tell you about people?
own.reply: Everything they won’t say. A man can tell you he’s generous. His expense report tells me the truth.

own.label: Ask how she learned accounts
own.player: How did you get into accounts?
own.reply: My father taught me double entry at ten with a box of buttons. Red buttons in, blue buttons out. I still see buttons when a column doesn’t balance.

own.label: Ask how long her face takes
own.player: How long does looking like that take you?
own.reply: Eleven minutes. If you look perfect, people assume you are and stop checking your work. It’s the single most useful thing I know.

own.label: Ask about her parents’ practice
own.player: Do your parents still work?
own.reply: They do the taxes for half the ranchers in the county, including the Whitlocks. My mother can tell a man is lying about his cattle from the way he holds his pen.

calls.label: Ask about the firm that doesn’t cater
calls.player: Tell me about the catering firm you flagged.
calls.reply: Late Service Catering. Paid the same every quarter, registered at the boarded-up weigh station at the old junction. I flagged it twice. Both flags vanished, removed with the treasurer’s login. So I keep a third copy, on paper, in a shoebox under my second-best heels.
calls.note: Yumi Tanaka says Late Service Catering is registered at the boarded weigh station at the old junction, and her warnings were deleted with the treasurer’s login.

calls.label: Ask if she’d share her third copy
calls.player: Would you let me see the third copy?
calls.reply: Only a page. The page with the trust’s payments on it. I’ll put it somewhere only you’ll look. If anyone asks, you found it in a shoe.

own.label: Ask about homicide work
own.player: What’s homicide work really like?
own.reply: Mostly sad families and bad coffee. The television version has better lighting and fewer forms.

own.label: Ask about the gala photo
own.player: I saw you in the gala photo in the paper.
own.reply: I was on duty, in a dress, because the board wanted security that blended in. The caption makes it look like I was a guest. I wasn’t. I was watching the door.
own.note: Officer Porter was on duty at the gala, watching the door, not attending as a guest.

own.label: Ask what she saw at the door
own.player: Did you see anything at the gala door?
own.reply: A man in a charity lanyard left by the kitchen, not the front. People who belong use the front.
own.note: Abigail Porter saw a man in a charity lanyard leave the gala through the kitchen.

own.label: Ask about the case she can’t forget
own.player: Is there a case you can’t forget?
own.reply: A girl the same age as my sister. We got the man. It didn’t help. Getting the man never helps the way you think it will.

own.label: Ask what she does to unwind
own.player: What do you do when you’re not working?
own.reply: I fix things. A toaster, a lamp, the station’s coffee machine twice. Something broken that wants to be fixed is very restful after people.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are the Porters a big Sunfall family?
own.reply: Gallery district money. Dad’s an architect who designed the club’s sailing annex and drank the fee. Mum is on the flower committee. I’d rather be in my workshop than at any of their tables.

own.label: Ask if it’s like television
own.player: Is homicide like it is on telly?
own.reply: The television version has better lighting and fewer forms. And on television the coffee is never this bad.

calls.label: Ask about the nine minutes
calls.player: Did you ever leave the door that night?
calls.reply: Nine minutes. My sergeant rang and told me to check the car park. In those nine minutes the kitchen door was unwatched and a grey car left. The sergeant was Vic Lowry. My log says I never moved. I wrote it that way, and I’ve been sick about it since.
calls.note: Abigail Porter left the door for nine minutes on gala night because Sergeant Vic Lowry rang her; a grey car left by the kitchen meanwhile.

calls.label: Ask about the note about her
calls.player: Someone’s trying to blame you, aren’t they?
calls.reply: An unsigned note, asking where Officer Porter drove E.C. after the benefit. I didn’t drive anyone. Somebody inside wants me to be the story.
calls.note: An unsigned note is trying to frame Abigail Porter for driving Elena Cross away.

own.label: Ask what a sergeant does
own.player: What does a sergeant actually do?
own.reply: I stop clever young detectives from doing clever things that end up in court. It’s babysitting with handcuffs.

own.label: Ask how the job has changed
own.player: Has the job changed much?
own.reply: We used to know the town. Now we know its phones. Fewer people talk to us and more people film us. I can’t decide if that’s progress.

own.label: Ask what her gut says
own.player: What does your gut say about Sunfall right now?
own.reply: That three separate things are happening and someone wants us to think they’re one. Or one thing wants us to think it’s three. I haven’t decided which.

own.label: Ask what the job did to her
own.player: What has the job done to you?
own.reply: It made me sit with my back to the wall in every restaurant. My ex said it was romantic at first. It isn’t, after a while.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are you from Sunfall?
own.reply: Born and bred. Dad drove the Moretti bakery’s bread van. Mum did the books for Ortega Repair. I knew every shop in this town by smell before I was ten.

own.label: Ask why she sits facing the door
own.player: Why do you always face the door?
own.reply: Back to the wall in every restaurant. My ex said it was romantic at first. It isn’t, after a while. It’s just tired.

own.label: Ask if she has a dog
own.player: Have you got pets?
own.reply: A dog I inherited from a dead colleague. He still waits by the door at six. So do I, some nights.

calls.label: Ask what’s in her drawer
calls.player: What do you keep in your desk drawer?
calls.reply: Eleven accident reports. Fourteen years. Every one a man who married a Bluebird and died inside three years: the dam, the junction, the reservoir, a heart attack at a dinner. I pulled them one at a time so nobody would notice. I’m waiting for a twelfth.
calls.note: Helen Markham keeps eleven accident reports: men who married Bluebirds and died within three years.

calls.label: Ask why she wants to see Diana Moore
calls.player: Why do you keep asking Diana Moore to lunch?
calls.reply: Because her second husband is report number nine, and she knows it, and one day she’ll be brave enough to eat a sandwich with a policewoman. I’ll keep asking.
calls.note: Helen Markham believes Diana Moore knows something about her husband Walter’s death.

own.label: Ask what undercover is like
own.player: What’s undercover work like?
own.reply: Exhausting. You spend your days being someone else and your nights remembering who you are. Dating is… complicated.

own.label: Ask if she lies on Hinge
own.player: Are you lying to me right now?
own.reply: Only about my job, sometimes. Never about whether I like someone. That’s the one thing I can’t fake.

own.label: Ask where she’s been working
own.player: Where have you been working lately?
own.reply: The motel strip. A room there was paid for in cash on the night of the gala by a man who used a fake name. I can’t say more. I’ve said too much.
own.note: Maria Vega says a motel room was paid for in cash under a fake name on the night of the gala.

own.label: Ask who she is when she isn’t undercover
own.player: Who are you when you’re not undercover?
own.reply: I’m still working that out. I’ve been other people so long that my own laugh sounds fake to me.

own.label: Ask where she sleeps
own.player: Where do you actually live?
own.reply: Two places. Lena’s flat above the bar, with a photo of a boyfriend who doesn’t exist. And my dad’s spare room, two nights a week, where he makes me eggs and doesn’t ask.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: What was your mum like?
own.reply: Founding-family girl who married a police sergeant against the committee. They never forgave her. She died when I was fourteen. She used to give fake names at restaurants as a joke. Mrs Swallow was her favourite.

own.label: Ask what undercover does to her
own.player: Does it change you, being someone else?
own.reply: My own laugh sounds fake to me now. Lena’s sounds real. That should worry someone. It worries my dad.

calls.label: Ask about the men on the strip
calls.player: Who are the men you’re watching?
calls.reply: Money lenders. Two days a week they work for the lodge up on the ridge. One’s called Brad Keller, and he has a key to the back door of the old Rialto. I don’t know why. I hate not knowing why.
calls.note: Maria Vega says the strip’s money lenders work for the lodge, and one, Brad Keller, has a key to the Rialto’s back door.

calls.label: Ask about room twelve
calls.player: Who paid for room twelve?
calls.reply: A woman, not a man. Cash. She signed the book Mrs Swallow, which was my mum’s joke name. I reported a man with a fake name, because a woman would send the station looking for Elena, and the station includes people I wouldn’t send looking for my cat.
calls.note: Maria Vega says room twelve was paid for in cash on gala night by a woman calling herself Mrs Swallow.

own.label: Ask what a police analyst does
own.player: What does a police analyst do?
own.reply: I find the pattern in the noise. Most crime is boring and repetitive. That’s what makes the strange ones stand out.

own.label: Ask if she likes quiet
own.player: You seem like someone who likes quiet.
own.reply: I do. Everyone else in the station talks. I listen to the numbers. They don’t interrupt.

own.label: Ask what pattern she sees
own.player: What’s the pattern you can’t stop thinking about?
own.reply: The bear calls spike on nights with no moon. So do the calls about lights at the old chapel. I don’t think the bear cares about the moon.
own.note: Keiko Nakamura says calls about lights at the old chapel spike on moonless nights.

own.label: Ask what pattern she’s noticed in Sunfall
own.player: What pattern have you noticed in Sunfall?
own.reply: Crime rises when the casino pays out and falls when the churches run their summer fairs. Make of that what you will.

own.label: Ask where she goes to think
own.player: Where do you go to think?
own.reply: The top floor of the library. The window faces the desert. Bethany lets me in after hours. It’s the quietest place in Sunfall, and I’ve measured.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Is your family local?
own.reply: My grandparents came to farm, and in the war they were put in a camp an hour from here. The town never mentions it. My grandmother mentions it every time she rings.

own.label: Ask what she reads
own.player: What do you read?
own.reply: Japanese crime novels my grandmother posts me. In those, the detective is usually right and usually lonely. I find that very relaxing.

calls.label: Ask when the next dark night is
calls.player: When’s the next night with no moon?
calls.reply: {night}. That’s when the calls about lights at the old chapel spike, every time, on my map. Bears don’t care about the moon. People do.

calls.label: Ask what else her map shows
calls.player: What else is on your map?
calls.reply: Eleven men dead within three years of one particular kind of wedding. And a grey car on the same streets the week after every benefit night. Nobody upstairs reads my reports.
calls.note: Keiko Nakamura’s map shows eleven men who died within three years of marrying into the Bluebirds.

own.label: Ask about her megaphone
own.player: Is it true you own three megaphones?
own.reply: Four. One is for emergencies. One is decorative. One makes a duck noise by accident. I love them all equally.

own.label: Ask if people blame her
own.player: Do people blame you for the trouble with Vale?
own.reply: Everyone looks at me first because I’m loud. Loud isn’t dangerous. Quiet is. Look at the quiet ones.
own.note: Jennifer says the dangerous people at the protests are the quiet ones, not the loud ones.

own.label: Ask about poetry slams
own.player: Do you do anything besides protests?
own.reply: Poetry slams. I came second last time to a man who just read his tax return angrily. Robbed.

own.label: Ask why she organises
own.player: Why do you organise?
own.reply: Because nobody else would book the hall. Leadership is mostly booking the hall.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A room in the housing co-op. Megaphones on a shelf, banners under the bed. Inez runs the place with a glare and I respect the glare.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Where are your family from?
own.reply: The hills. Logging people, came down with nothing and an opinion. Dad drives a timber truck. Mum teaches drama at the hill school, which explains the megaphones.

views.speakers: I protest Vale’s speakers because they make kids on our campus feel small. Say what you like, but don’t pretend it doesn’t land on real people.
views.campus: Best protest yet! We had a drum. Nobody could play the drum. It was beautiful.
views.police: They know my name, my face and my megaphone. We’re practically pen pals.

calls.label: Ask about the drum nobody can play
calls.player: Where did that drum at the protests come from?
calls.reply: A man in a charity lanyard donated it. Said he admired the cause. Nobody can play it and the case is weirdly heavy at the bottom. I keep meaning to look. I never have. Loud people don’t look at things, apparently.
calls.note: Jennifer Tate says the protest drum was donated by a man in a charity lanyard, and its case is oddly heavy at the bottom.

own.label: Ask about her books
own.player: Is it true your flat is full of books?
own.reply: Floor to ceiling. Most of them are about how ordinary people finally said no. History is a list of people who stopped asking nicely.

own.label: Ask why she’s an activist
own.player: Why did you get into activism?
own.reply: Because I watched polite people lose, again and again, to powerful people who don’t care about polite.

own.label: Ask if she’s ever scared
own.player: Do you ever scare yourself?
own.reply: Anger is a tool. You only get scared of a tool when you don’t know how to hold it.

own.label: Ask about the Back Row
own.player: People mention something called the Back Row.
own.reply: People say a lot of things at meetings. The back row is where you sit when you’re done talking. That’s all it is. Isn’t it?

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Where are you from?
own.reply: The gallery district, which I don’t say on campus. Mum’s on the museum board. Dad drafts wills for rich people. I grew up reading the endings of other people’s lives on his desk.

own.label: Ask what she does for money
own.player: What do you actually do for money?
own.reply: A campaigns job for a non-profit in the city, done from my sofa. It pays the rent. The real work happens in the evenings.

views.speakers: Vale invites men who say cruelty is honesty. Every lecture tells a room full of nineteen-year-olds who matters and who doesn’t. At some point, talking about it stops being enough.
views.campus: Protest is the polite version. The university has had its polite version.
views.police: They protect property. Ask them what they protect people from.

calls.label: Ask about the will she read
calls.player: You said you read a will once?
calls.reply: Walter Hallam’s. My father drafted it. I know exactly what the Foundation is and what it does to the men who marry into it. But the Bluebirds are old and slow, and a movement needs a target it can reach. They can wait.
calls.note: Vanessa Greer read Walter Hallam’s will, drafted by her father, and knows what the Foundation does to the men who marry in.

own.label: Ask what it’s like working for Vale
own.player: What’s it like working for Professor Vale?
own.reply: He’s brilliant, vain and exhausting. I keep his diary, so I know where he’ll be before he does. That’s more power than people think.

own.label: Ask which side she’s on
own.player: So which side are you on, the protesters or Vale?
own.reply: I’m on the side of people who read the whole book before they burn it. Which, in this town, makes me lonely.

own.label: Ask about the people at the back of the room
own.player: Who are the people who sit at the back of the campus meetings?
own.reply: Funny you’d ask me that. They’re just students. Very serious students. I wouldn’t worry about them, if I were you.
own.note: Allison Kent got oddly defensive when asked about the people at the back of the campus meetings.

own.label: Ask what she’d write in her own diary
own.player: If you kept your own diary, what would be in it?
own.reply: Mostly other people’s appointments, sadly. I’ve organised a famous man’s life so long I forgot to schedule mine.

own.label: Ask about her own diary
own.player: Do you keep a diary of your own?
own.reply: In a code I invented at fourteen. Nobody has cracked it. Nobody has tried, which is the same thing and also sadder.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What did your dad do?
own.reply: He ran a stationery shop that printed the Foundation’s programmes until they went elsewhere. He died of the loss, slowly, over six years. I spent them being brilliant at a man who didn’t see me.

calls.label: Ask who else drives Vale’s car
calls.player: Does anyone else drive Professor Vale’s car?
calls.reply: Dr Pemberton borrows it on the days after public events. I arrange the loan myself. I haven’t told anyone that. I’m not sure I mind what that means.
calls.note: Allison Kent says Dr Hal Pemberton borrows Professor Vale’s car on the days after public events, and she arranges it.

own.label: Ask about her thesis
own.player: What’s your thesis on?
own.reply: Water rights in the desert. Who owns the rain. It sounds boring until you realise the answer is whoever got there first with a lawyer.

own.label: Ask how she’s doing
own.player: How are you doing, really?
own.reply: I don’t sleep much. I check the lock twice. It’s probably just deadlines. Probably.

own.label: Ask about her friends at the meetings
own.player: What are the people at your meetings like?
own.reply: Most of them are lovely. A few of them sit at the back and never vote, and when they look at me I feel like I’ve already said too much.
own.note: Rosa is frightened of a few people who sit at the back of the campus meetings.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Is your family nearby?
own.reply: My mum’s an hour south. She thinks I’m studying. I am studying. Mostly.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: Water people, an hour south. Grandad lost a well to a lawyer in a suit, which is why I study water. Dad fixes pumps. Mum cleans for a judge. They think I’m studying. I am, mostly.

own.label: Ask why her lights are always off
own.player: Why are your lights always off at night?
own.reply: I sit in the dark and check the lock. Twice. It’s probably deadlines. Probably.

own.label: Ask what her supervisor wants
own.player: What does your supervisor think of the thesis?
own.reply: He’s asked me to soften the part where I name who owns the rain. It was the Shawcrosses. Whoever got there first with a lawyer.

views.campus: I agree with the protests. I just don’t agree with everyone in them.
views.speakers: I think Vale’s guests are wrong. I also think some of the people who hate them have stopped seeing the professor as a person. That scares me more than any speech.

calls.label: Ask about the man with the poems
calls.player: Who’s leaving poems outside your seminar?
calls.reply: He was on our course before they asked him to leave. He speaks to the porters in verse. His name’s Theon. He signs the poems Orsino, and he’s using someone else’s photographs. Campus security says there’s nothing to be done.
calls.note: Rosa Gutierrez says the man leaving poems was on her course: his name is Theon.

own.label: Ask how she runs the parish
own.player: How do you keep the whole parish running?
own.reply: Lists. Lists of lists. A rota for the flowers, a rota for the food pantry, and a rota for the rotas. Chaos is a choice.

own.label: Ask about the guitar dispute
own.player: What’s really going on with the bishop and the guitars?
own.reply: The bishop wants to modernise us. We have sung the same Mass in that chapel since before he was born. I have written him four letters. He has replied to none.

own.label: Ask why she isn’t married
own.player: Can I ask why you’re not married?
own.reply: Because nobody has yet passed my questions. I don’t mean to sound proud. I mean that marriage is forever, and I take forever seriously.

own.label: Ask about the old vigils
own.player: Do the Sisters still hold vigils?
own.reply: When there’s need. A vigil needs a leader, keys, someone on the door and enough voices. I’ve organised harder things. Never a more frightening one.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: Is your mother still in the parish?
own.reply: Alive, sharp, and at every Mass in a hat that has opinions. My great-grandparents gave St Brigid’s its organ. My mother behaves as if she’s still paying for it.

own.label: Ask about her morning walk
own.player: What do you do first thing?
own.reply: I walk the parish. I know which lights are on and which should be. A coordinator who doesn’t walk is just a woman with a clipboard.

own.label: Ask if she’s ever silly
own.player: Are you ever not stern?
own.reply: Ask Teresa or Sophia. Nobody else has seen it and I intend to keep it that way. I do a very good impression of the bishop’s secretary.

own.label: Ask about the bishop’s review
own.player: What’s this review of the Sisters about?
own.reply: The chancellor’s letter came the week after our caretaker stopped coming to Mass. The guitars are an excuse. Somebody wants our land, and our papers. I have put the papers where the review won’t find them, and I don’t have the key. Truthfully.
own.note: Margaret Holloway says the bishop’s review of the Sisters is about their land and papers, which she has hidden.

views.believe: In order. God made an orderly world and people keep untidying it.
views.campus: Young people shouting is not new. Young people refusing to listen at all is.
views.sisters: We are not a museum. We are a household. We just happen to have very old furniture.

own.label: Ask about teaching
own.player: What’s it like teaching at the parish school?
own.reply: Twenty-two eight-year-olds and one class hamster who is, theologically speaking, a menace.

own.label: Ask about her grandmother’s shop
own.player: Your grandmother has a shop?
own.reply: Bellamy & Daughters Antiques. She’s sold rings to half the parish. She says every ring has a story and she knows most of them.

own.label: Ask about the old chapel
own.player: What’s the story of the old chapel outside town?
own.reply: The old mission chapel lost its bell in a storm, long ago. The old women say it was the night the bell forgot its voice. Children dare each other to go there.
own.note: Teresa says the old mission chapel is the one whose bell forgot its voice.

own.label: Ask about her favourite saint
own.player: Do you have a favourite saint?
own.reply: Saint Brigid, of course. Patroness of our chapel, and she once turned bathwater into beer for visitors. Hospitality is holy.

own.label: Ask about living above the shop
own.player: What’s it like living above an antiques shop?
own.reply: Granny’s cuckoo clocks go off at different times, so phone calls are a lottery. If you hear a bird, that’s not me, that’s eighteen-forties Bavaria.

own.label: Ask about her grandparents’ wedding
own.player: How did your grandparents meet?
own.reply: Granddad Walter dropped the ring in the font at their wedding, fifty-one years ago, and Father fished it out with the aspergillum. Granny still says it was the most blessed ring in the county.

own.label: Ask about her exams
own.player: Are you a strict teacher?
own.reply: Ruthless. Twenty-two eight-year-olds know the seven sacraments in order or they don’t get the hamster for the weekend. It works on adults too, I find.

own.label: Ask who asked her about the bell tower
own.player: Did anyone ever ask you about the old bell tower?
own.reply: A girl in black at a parish open day, two years ago, with a notebook. Victoria, she said. I told her which chapel’s bell forgot its voice, and why the Sisters keep vigil on the new moon, because I answer questions. She thanked me and wrote it all down. I think I gave somebody a calendar.
own.note: Teresa Bellamy told Victoria Blackwood which chapel’s bell went silent and why the Sisters keep vigil on the new moon.

own.label: Ask when the next vigil is
own.player: When is the Sisters’ next vigil?
own.reply: On the new moon: {night}. We keep the vigil because once, long ago, other women kept something else on those nights. Come and stand at the back if you like. Bring a coat.

views.believe: That small kindnesses are how the world gets mended, one stitch at a time.
views.goths: One of them asked me about the old bell tower once. She wasn’t curious. She was taking notes.

own.label: Ask about her parish work
own.player: What do you do for the parish?
own.reply: I keep the accounts and the minutes. Nobody notices me unless something’s missing, which is how I like it.

own.label: Ask what she prays for
own.player: What do you pray for?
own.reply: Mostly for other people. Sometimes, when I’m brave, for a husband who’d be kind to a quiet woman.

own.label: Ask what scares her
own.player: What scares you?
own.reply: Being asked to be brave in public. I’ll do anything, so long as I don’t have to do it in front of people.

own.label: Ask what kindness costs her
own.player: What does kindness cost you?
own.reply: Sleep, mostly. And sometimes pride. You can’t help people and also need them to say thank you.

own.label: Ask about her grandmother’s sewing box
own.player: What’s in the sewing box?
own.reply: My grandmother sewed St Brigid’s altar linens for fifty years. I mend them now with her needles. Some of the stitches are older than the town hall.

own.label: Ask how she came to the accounts
own.player: How did you start keeping the accounts?
own.reply: My father kept them before me. He died of a stroke at the desk, and I took the ledger out of his hands. Literally. I’ve kept it since.

own.label: Ask why she checks everything twice
own.player: Do you really check everything twice?
