own.reply: Twice, and then once more when nobody is looking. Mistakes in a parish ledger aren’t mistakes. They’re somebody’s supper.

own.label: Ask what she found in the accounts
own.player: Did you find something in the parish accounts?
own.reply: A payment to a company called Halcyon Ridge Consultancy, signed by the bishop’s own chancellor, hidden under the garden line. It means the review was bought. I’ve shown nobody, because showing it means going before the king.
own.note: Evelyn Rosales found the bishop’s chancellor signed the parish’s payment to Halcyon Ridge Consultancy, so the review against the Sisters was bought.

own.label: Ask what the minutes say lately
own.player: Anything unusual in the minutes lately?
own.reply: Pantry stock. One more for supper, upstairs, until further notice. That’s all it says, and that’s all I’ll say.
own.note: Evelyn Rosales’s pantry minutes record one more for supper, upstairs, until further notice.

own.label: Ask what she’s investigating
own.player: What are you investigating at the moment?
own.reply: Three stories, two of which might be the same story. That’s the best feeling in this job.

own.label: Ask why she became a reporter
own.player: Why become a reporter?
own.reply: Because my school covered up a teacher who hurt kids, and the local paper didn’t. I thought: never again, not on my watch.

own.label: Ask what her sources say
own.player: What are your sources saying about the gala?
own.reply: That the money went missing before Elena did. Follow the money and you find the person. That’s always the order.
own.note: Hannah Webb’s sources say the money went missing before Elena Cross did.

own.label: Ask if the truth still matters
own.player: Does the truth still matter to people?
own.reply: It matters to about nine readers and my grandmother. I write for them. Everyone else wants a team to cheer for.

own.label: Ask what her flat looks like
own.player: What does an investigative reporter’s flat look like?
own.reply: A bedsit with a wall of string. I eat at my desk. Once a week I sleep at my grandmother’s, and she reads every word I’ve written aloud and marks it in red.

own.label: Ask who raised her
own.player: Who brought you up?
own.reply: My grandmother, on the railway side. Dad was a guard on the last passenger train. Mum went to the coast. Gran was a reader, so I became a writer out of self-defence.

own.label: Ask if anyone tried to reach Elena
own.player: Did anyone try to get a message to Elena?
own.reply: Our front desk took one for her the night of the benefit. A frightened woman, initials only. I made a copy before the slip went upstairs. You can have it if you protect her.

calls.label: Ask what her third story is
calls.player: What’s the third story you won’t name?
calls.reply: The husbands. Eleven names, matched to blue ribbons at the Cemetery Chapel. I haven’t written a word, because eleven dead men with nothing provable is a libel. The first name is Ellis Dane. He sponsored the youth orchestra I played in at twelve, and the next year his name was gone from the programme.
calls.note: Hannah Webb has eleven names of men who married Bluebirds and died; the first is Ellis Dane.

own.label: Ask what an editor does
own.player: What does an editor actually do?
own.reply: Decide what Sunfall knows tomorrow. It’s a lot of power for someone who can’t decide what to have for lunch.

own.label: Ask about the state of the news
own.player: Is the news business dying?
own.reply: It’s being eaten by people who give their opinions away for free. Opinions are cheap. Facts cost shoe leather, and nobody wants to pay for shoes.

own.label: Ask why she spiked a story
own.player: Did you spike a story about the gala?
own.reply: I spiked a photo. A board member rang me at home that night. I told myself it was legal advice. I don’t sleep well.
own.note: Fiona Blake admits she spiked a gala photo after a board member rang her at home.

own.label: Ask what she’d never put on the front page
own.player: What would you never put on the front page?
own.reply: A child’s face, a grieving widow, and anything I can’t prove twice. I lose a lot of stories that way. I sleep fine.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Do you ever leave the newsroom?
own.reply: I live directly above it. Literally. A bed I fall into and a phone that rings. Editing is a punishment I chose, because I’d rather chase a mystery than sit still, and now I sit still and send other people.

own.label: Ask about her family and the paper
own.player: Has your family always run the Daily?
own.reply: Grandad owned it. He sold it to a chain, which sold it to a man who owes money to the wrong people. I’m the last Blake in the building and the only reason it’s still a paper.

calls.label: Ask who really owns the paper
calls.player: Who actually owns the Daily?
calls.reply: A man in the city who owes the Halcyon Ridge Trust. If I print the wrong front page, the Trust calls the debt, the Daily closes, and Sunfall has no paper at all. Every day for a month I’ve decided a compromised paper beats none. I’m not sure.
calls.note: Fiona Blake says the Daily’s owner is in debt to the Halcyon Ridge Trust.

calls.label: Ask about the photograph in her desk
calls.player: Do you still have the photo you spiked?
calls.reply: In my desk. Table 9, the treasurer’s table, with a face that isn’t on any guest list. If I give it to you I’ve given it to nobody. Understood? Good. Don’t frame it.

own.label: Ask about freelancing
own.player: What’s freelancing like?
own.reply: Feast or famine. Mostly famine. I once sold a photo of the bear for more than a month of real journalism.

own.label: Ask what she’s writing
own.player: Are you writing anything?
own.reply: A novel about Sunfall that I’ll never finish. Everyone in town is in it. You might be in it now. Behave.

own.label: Ask about her motel photos
own.player: You photograph the motel strip?
own.reply: For a project. In one shot from the gala night, there’s a woman in a blue dress in Room 12’s window. Elena wore blue.
own.note: Linh Tran has a photo from gala night of a woman in a blue dress in a motel window. Elena wore blue.

own.label: Ask if freelancing is freedom
own.player: Is freelancing really freedom?
own.reply: It’s freedom to not get paid on time. But nobody tells me what to think, and that’s worth being broke.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: Above the laundromat on Sunfall Road. Thin walls, a radiator that sings at night, and a neighbour who sells houses and another who plays pool. If you live there too, hello, neighbour. Turn your music down.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: We had a restaurant until the casino’s rents ate it. Dad cooks at the casino now, for the people who priced him out. Mum does nails. They’re funnier about it than I am.

calls.label: Ask what she saw at the motel later
calls.player: Did you go back to the motel?
calls.reply: At night, more than once. Room twelve was empty. Room nine is never rented, but there’s a light in it sometimes, and once a man in a cloak, reading at the window. I put him in my novel. He frightened my novel.
calls.note: Linh Tran saw a man in a cloak reading in the window of motel room nine, which is never rented.

calls.label: Ask what’s spooking her about her novel
calls.player: Why does your novel scare you?
calls.reply: Three chapters ago I wrote a scene in a weigh station, a woman going out through a window. I thought I made it up. Then the paper started printing my chapters back at me.

own.label: Ask about DJing
own.player: What’s it like DJing the goth night?
own.reply: Like conducting a funeral where everyone’s dancing. I live for it.

own.label: Ask what’s wrong with music now
own.player: What’s wrong with music now?
own.reply: Everything sounds like it was designed to be skipped. The old songs were built to be lived in.

own.label: Ask about the special set
own.player: Has anyone asked you for a special set?
own.reply: Victoria wants me to play a twenty-minute drone at the Midnight Show, starting exactly when the moon disappears. She paid in advance. Nobody pays in advance.
own.note: Victoria paid Alice Wren in advance for a long drone set timed to the moonless night.

own.label: Ask about the best silence she’s heard
own.player: What’s the best silence you’ve ever heard?
own.reply: The second after the last record ends at a good night. Two hundred people standing still. Then the lights come up and it’s gone.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: The railway side. Dad worked the signal box. I can hear a train before you can see it, which is very useful for a DJ and nothing else.

own.label: Ask about her loop pedal
own.player: What’s the loop pedal for?
own.reply: A job. I bought it for cash at the music shop and tested it once. I haven’t switched it on since. Some gear you buy and then avoid looking at.

calls.label: Ask when the drone starts
calls.player: When exactly is this drone meant to start?
calls.reply: The second the moon goes. {night}. Twenty minutes, then the best silence there is. She paid in advance. Nobody pays in advance.

calls.label: Ask what’s on the tape she was given
calls.player: What’s actually on the mix she gave you?
calls.reply: Under the drone, on her cassette, there’s a round for nine voices and a bell. I know that bell’s note. It’s the one on Odette Price’s old radio reel from the Old Mission fair. I think I’ve been hired to play the founders’ music back into the Old Mission.
calls.note: Alice Wren says the rite’s music hides a round for nine voices and the Old Mission’s bell, the same as on Odette Price’s old radio reel.

own.label: Ask about the shop
own.player: What do you sell at the shop?
own.reply: Velvet, silver and despair, at reasonable prices.

own.label: Ask if she breaks hearts
own.player: Are you a heartbreaker?
own.reply: I leave before it gets serious. It’s kinder. Probably. I’ve never stayed long enough to find out.

own.label: Ask who buys the crescent pendants
own.player: Who buys the crescent pendants?
own.reply: We sold thirty in a week to people who don’t look like goths. Accountants. A man in a charity lanyard. That’s not fashion. That’s a uniform.
own.note: Piper Nocturne’s shop sold thirty crescent pendants in a week, including to a man in a charity lanyard.

own.label: Ask what she keeps from her exes
own.player: Do you keep anything from your exes?
own.reply: One thing each. A lighter, a ticket stub, a terrible poem. It’s a small museum of men who were wrong about me.

own.label: Ask how she came to the shop
own.player: How did you end up working at the shop?
own.reply: My aunt owns it. She took me in when Mum died, when I was fourteen, and let me rename myself. I was born Piper Dunne in the trailer park behind the drive-in. Don’t tell the Old Quarter.

own.label: Ask what’s in the drawer she never opens
own.player: What’s in the drawer you don’t open?
own.reply: A crescent pendant somebody gave me three years ago, before there were thirty of them. It was a present then. Now it’s a uniform.

calls.label: Ask who’s in the shop’s book
calls.player: Who did you sell the pendants to?
calls.reply: My aunt makes me write every sale in the book. There’s a Beaumont in it. A Shawcross. Two Pells. Since when do Pells wear silver moons?
calls.note: Piper Nocturne’s shop book shows crescent pendants sold to a Beaumont, a Shawcross and two Pells.

calls.label: Ask how well she knows Victoria
calls.player: How well do you know Victoria?
calls.reply: Better than the scene thinks. We weren’t friends. We were more than that, once. She still knows exactly how to ask me for things.
calls.note: Piper Nocturne and Victoria Blackwood were lovers, not just friends.

own.label: Ask about tattooing
own.player: What’s the strangest tattoo you’ve done?
own.reply: A man’s ex-wife’s name, changed into a cactus. He cried. I didn’t charge him extra for the cactus.

own.label: Ask how people treat her
own.player: Do people judge you for how you look?
own.reply: Every day. The same people who say be yourself cross the road when I am.

own.label: Ask about the crescent tattoos
own.player: Has anyone asked for a crescent tattoo?
own.reply: Three people this month, same design, same spot inside the wrist. They wouldn’t say why. I turned the last one away.
own.note: Zara Brooks was asked for the same crescent tattoo, inside the wrist, three times this month.

own.label: Ask which tattoo she regrets
own.player: Do you regret any of your tattoos?
own.reply: One. A name. Not his, mine. I got my own name on my wrist at eighteen so I’d never forget it. I’ve never needed reminding.

own.label: Ask about the name on her wrist
own.player: Whose name is on your wrist?
own.reply: Mine. So I never forget it. People laugh. I’ve watched a lot of people forget who they were in this town.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Have you got family in Sunfall?
own.reply: My cousin Arielle. Dolores raised us both at the Lucky Cactus counter. I walked Arielle to school every day. I still would.

calls.label: Ask who got the crescent tattoo
calls.player: Who got the crescent inside the wrist?
calls.reply: Two girls, Hex and Ivy. The third was Sorrel. I turned her away, because a mark you can’t explain is a mark somebody else owns. I drew the flyer’s crescent, too. I’ve started to understand what it invites people to.
calls.note: Zara Brooks tattooed the crescent on Hex Morrow and Ivy Sable and turned Sorrel Vane away.

women.name: Maya Serrano
women.look: Olive skin, dark curls in a high ponytail, teal scrubs and a white zip hoodie

own.label: Ask about her shifts
own.player: What happened on your last shift?
own.reply: Cactus spines, a man who swallowed a key, and a grandmother who flirted with every doctor. Standard.

own.label: Ask about the café idea
own.player: You want to open a café?
own.reply: With my sister. She bakes, I’d do the coffee and the shouting. Somewhere with no laptops after dark, just people talking.

own.label: Ask about the patient she recognised
own.player: Did you recognise a patient?
own.reply: A man came in with burns on his hands, and I knew his face from the newspaper. He gave a different name. I told no one. I’m telling you.
own.note: Maya Serrano treated a man with burnt hands whose face she knew from the newspaper; he gave a false name.

own.label: Ask what she does after a hard shift
own.player: What do you do after a really hard shift?
own.reply: Sit in my car in the hospital car park and eat a whole packet of biscuits. Then I drive home and tell nobody.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are your family nurses?
own.reply: Mum nursed at the hospital for thirty years and Dad drove the ambulance. I grew up in the back of it. My first word was probably clear.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you have a sister?
own.reply: Rosa, no relation to the student, I always have to say. She bakes. One day we’re opening a café, no laptops after dark, just people talking. I’ll do coffee and shouting.

calls.label: Ask who the burned man was
calls.player: Who was the man with the burned hands?
calls.reply: Caleb Marsh. I knew his face from the paper. He gave another name. His sister came and collected him. The chart says garden-centre accelerant, because the doctor wrote what he smelled.
calls.note: Maya Serrano treated Caleb Marsh’s burned hands under a false name; his sister collected him.

calls.label: Ask about men from the ridge
calls.player: Do men from the ridge come in?
calls.reply: With quarry injuries that aren’t quarry injuries. The first one I saw was a dog bite. The dog was the lodge’s. The night ward keeps a list now.
calls.note: Maya Serrano says injured men from the ridge come into A&E with wounds that aren’t from the quarry.

women.name: Jocelyn Reed
women.look: Dark skin, cropped natural curls, royal-blue blazer and a tiny blue ribbon

own.label: Ask about her job
own.player: What does a compliance officer do?
own.reply: I ask grown adults for receipts and they look at me as if I’ve asked for a kidney. It’s thankless, and I’m very good at it.

own.label: Ask about her hobby
own.player: What do you do to relax?
own.reply: I restore old furniture. Strip the paint, find the honest wood underneath. It’s the opposite of my job: the furniture wants to be found out.

own.label: Ask what keeps her up at night
own.player: What keeps you up at night?
own.reply: I have a second copy of a donation ledger. If I publish it, my career is over. If I don’t, I’m complicit. So mostly I lie awake and sand chairs.
own.note: Jocelyn Reed has a second copy of a donation ledger she is afraid to publish.

own.label: Ask about the worst couple she ever set up
own.player: What’s the worst couple you ever set up?
own.reply: A vegan and a butcher. They’re married now with three children. I don’t understand anything any more.

own.label: Ask how she got into finance
own.player: How did you end up in compliance?
own.reply: I worked nights on a hotel desk through a finance degree. You learn everything about people at three in the morning. Mostly that they think the receipt won’t matter.

own.label: Ask where she’s from
own.player: Where are you from originally?
own.reply: A town on the coast. Mum was the church secretary. Dad was the kind of man who made the church secretary cry. I left at seventeen and didn’t look back, except constantly.

own.label: Ask about her favourite restoration
own.player: What’s the best thing you’ve ever restored?
own.reply: An ottoman. Seven coats of paint and underneath, walnut. Hollow inside, too. Useful.

calls.label: Ask about the copy she can’t sleep over
calls.player: What’s the copy you lie awake about?
calls.reply: The donation ledger from the year before the benefit, with the trust’s payments still in it, before somebody rewrote the official one. If I publish it I’m finished. If I don’t, I’m them. It’s in the ottoman. I’ll give you one page and then I never met you.

calls.label: Ask what else she found
calls.player: Have you found anything else?
calls.reply: The catering invoices, the firm that never caters, are in the events director’s own handwriting. Dorian Kell writes his sevens the European way. So do the invoices.
calls.note: Jocelyn Reed says the Late Service Catering invoices are in Dorian Kell’s handwriting.

women.name: Priya Nair
women.look: Brown skin, dark side braid, tortoiseshell glasses, sage cardigan and long skirt

own.label: Ask about the parish reading room
own.player: Tell me about the parish reading room.
own.reply: Three shelves, two armchairs and a radiator that sings. The council wants to close it. The old men who read the papers there have nowhere else to go.

own.label: Ask about the hymn books
own.player: You restore hymn books?
own.reply: Handwritten ones, from when the chapel had a choir of forty. The ink fades, but the faith in those margins is still loud.

own.label: Ask about the strange book
own.player: Have you found anything strange in the collection?
own.reply: An old missal with a crescent drawn inside the cover and a line of Latin that isn’t from any prayer I know. Someone borrowed it last month and brought it back changed.
own.note: Priya Nair found a crescent and unknown Latin drawn inside a missal someone borrowed and returned.

own.label: Ask what book she’d save from a fire
own.player: Which book would you save from a fire?
own.reply: My grandmother’s missal. It’s falling apart and full of her notes in the margins. Her handwriting is the closest thing I have to her voice.

own.label: Ask about living above the reading room
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: Above the reading room. I think of it as the top of a lighthouse. The radiator sings, the old men come, and the books go out and come back changed.

own.label: Ask what her family think
own.player: What does your family think of the reading room?
own.reply: My parents are doctors in the city and think it’s a hobby. My grandmother endowed it to thank God for a daughter who got better. I think of it as keeping her promise.

own.label: Ask who borrowed the missal
own.player: Who borrowed the book with the crescent in it?
own.reply: Someone on a dead man’s card. Harold Oakley’s. A young man. It came back with a crescent drawn inside the cover and a line of Latin in a new hand. I won’t report a reader. But I can tell you the card is still being used.
own.note: Priya Nair says a young man borrowing on the late Harold Oakley’s reading card returned a missal with a crescent and new Latin inside.

women.name: Inez Morales
women.look: Amber skin, wavy chestnut bob, turquoise eyeshadow, corduroy jacket and vintage band T-shirt

own.label: Ask about campus housing
own.player: How bad is student housing here?
own.reply: Students sleeping in cars, while the university builds a meditation garden. You can’t meditate in a Honda Civic. I’ve tried.

own.label: Ask about her gig posters
own.player: You make gig posters?
own.reply: Screen-printed, illegal, beautiful. The goths pay in drinks and the punks pay in nothing. It’s the only honest economy in town.

own.label: Ask who funds her co-op
own.player: Who funds your housing co-operative?
own.reply: We got a donation from a charity with no office and no website. It saved us. I’m scared to find out who it really was.
own.note: Inez Morales’s housing co-op received money from a charity with no office and no website.

own.label: Ask what she really thinks about landlords
own.player: What do you really think about landlords?
own.reply: That most of them are just retired couples who were scared about money. That’s the bit nobody on my side likes hearing.

own.label: Ask where she sleeps
own.player: Where’s your room in the co-op?
own.reply: By the front door. The organiser sleeps by the door. That way I hear every late key and every landlord.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you have siblings?
own.reply: Isabel, who trains horses at the Whitlock ranch. We’re a farrier’s daughters who went opposite ways. We ring each other every night and argue about who got it right.

calls.label: Ask who really owns the co-op
calls.player: Who really saved the co-op?
calls.reply: The charity with no office is the trust on the ridge, and the gift was a loan secured on the building. They own our roof now. If I say so out loud, forty students are sleeping in cars by the end of the week.
calls.note: Inez Morales says the trust on the ridge holds a loan secured on the student co-op’s building.

women.name: Rowan Pike
women.look: Pale skin, silver-black undercut, grey-green eyes, subtle tattoos and crescent jewellery

own.label: Ask about running the studio
own.player: What’s it like running your own studio?
own.reply: Like being a priest with needles. People tell me things they’ve never told anyone. Then they pay me.

own.label: Ask about the investor
own.player: Someone wants to buy your studio?
own.reply: A wellness brand wants to turn it into a chain. Tattoos as self-care. I’d rather burn it down.

own.label: Ask about the key
own.player: Did someone leave something at the studio?
own.reply: A girl from Victoria’s circle left a key on the counter. Old, iron, too big for any door I know. I haven’t given it back.
own.note: Rowan Pike has an old iron key left at her studio by a girl from Victoria’s circle.

own.label: Ask what she won’t tattoo
own.player: What won’t you tattoo?
own.reply: Faces of exes and hate symbols. Everything else, if you’re sober and you’ve thought about it for a week.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Is Madison at the diner your sister?
own.reply: My little sister. I raised her from ten, after Mum died and Dad went away. She thinks I’m strict. I am. She’s still the best thing I’ve made.

own.label: Ask what happened to her father
own.player: Where’s your dad now?
own.reply: He kept the lenders’ book on the motel strip and got caught. I was nineteen. I still have the book. It has interesting names in it.

calls.label: Ask what the iron key fits
calls.player: Have you worked out what that key opens?
calls.reply: My mum’s old friend described a door to her once, thirty years ago, and I was in the room. The Old Mission’s crypt door. Iron, too big, a lock like a fist. That’s what the girl left on my counter.
calls.note: Rowan Pike believes the iron key Sorrel Vane left her opens the Old Mission’s crypt door.

calls.label: Ask about the wellness brand’s offer
calls.player: Who’s really behind the investor?
calls.reply: Page four of their offer. Small print. The Halcyon Ridge Trust. They want the studio, the old cinema, the whole street. And Dad’s lenders’ book has a Blackwood in it, in debt.
calls.note: Rowan Pike says the wellness brand’s offer for her studio is backed by the Halcyon Ridge Trust.

women.name: Camille Baptiste
women.look: Deep brown skin, dark locs tied in a scarf, olive utility jacket and silver compact-camera strap

own.label: Ask about her motel photographs
own.player: Why photograph old motels?
own.reply: Because they’re where America keeps its secrets. Every motel sign is a promise someone broke.

own.label: Ask for a story
own.player: Tell me a Sunfall story.
own.reply: A woman ran the diner for forty years and never once took a day off. The day she died, the jukebox played her song by itself. Everyone swears it. I believe it.

own.label: Ask what her gala photo shows
own.player: What did you see in your gala photographs?
own.reply: A face at Table 9 who isn’t on the official guest list. Not a waiter, not a guest. Someone who wasn’t meant to be remembered.
own.note: Camille Baptiste photographed someone at Table 9 who isn’t on the official guest list.

own.label: Ask what photography taught her about people
own.player: What has photography taught you about people?
own.reply: That everyone has one honest face and they only show it when they think nobody’s looking. My job is to be nobody.

own.label: Ask about her flat
own.player: What’s on your walls?
own.reply: Motel signs. Vacancy, No Vacancy, one that just says Ice. Every motel sign is a promise someone broke.

own.label: Ask who taught her photography
own.player: Who taught you to take pictures?
own.reply: My grandfather photographed weddings. My mother photographed the ones he wouldn’t. I learned both, which is why I can make anyone look married or divorced.

own.label: Ask why her stories never end
own.player: Why do you never finish a story?
own.reply: Because then you’d stop listening. Editors and men both come back for the ending. I keep it in my pocket.

calls.label: Ask whose face is in her photograph
calls.player: Who is the face at Table 9?
calls.reply: I went up the lodge road with a long lens and photographed a car. Same face. Lyle Marchbanks. He’s on no guest list anywhere and at every table that matters. The same roll has a girl from the club with her hand on his arm.
calls.note: Camille Baptiste identified the face at Table 9 as Lyle Marchbanks, photographed again on the lodge road.

calls.label: Ask if she’d share the frame
calls.player: Could I see that frame?
calls.reply: A cropped print. Not the whole roll, I’m not mad. Enough that you’ll know him if you see him. Treat it like it’s radioactive.

women.name: Tessa Larkin
women.look: Freckled fair skin, copper-red braids, bright coral top and faded jeans

own.label: Ask about the lizard
own.player: Did you get the lizard out of your kitchen?
own.reply: Eventually. His name is Gregory now. He lives in a shoebox and judges me.

own.label: Ask about her clay birds
own.player: You make clay birds?
own.reply: Terrible ones. They look like potatoes with opinions. I keep making them because I love birds and I’m not good at anything else, artistically.

own.label: Ask what she saw near the enclosure
own.player: Did you see something near the animal enclosure?
own.reply: A van with no plates parked by the bear trap the rangers didn’t set. Two men were checking a laptop. They drove off when I waved.
own.note: Tessa Larkin saw a van with no plates and two men with a laptop by an unofficial bear trap.

own.label: Ask what wild animals teach her
own.player: What do wild animals teach you?
own.reply: That you can’t love something into staying. You feed it, you heal it, and you open the box and let it go.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A caravan at the rescue centre, with Gregory and whatever’s come in this week. Right now a hawk with a wing and a fox with opinions.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: We had an orchard until the water went to a rich family. Dad’s bitter, Mum keeps bees. At fourteen Dad told me you can’t love something into staying. He meant the orchard.

calls.label: Ask about the Foundation’s offer
calls.player: What’s the Foundation offering the rescue centre?
calls.reply: A permanent home on the ridge, by the lodge, with a grant. Page four says our animals must be available for their educational programme. That means they want a licensed place to keep a bear.
calls.note: Tessa Larkin says the Foundation’s offer to house the rescue centre on the ridge would let the lodge legally keep a bear.

calls.label: Ask what was on the men’s laptop
calls.player: What was on that laptop by the trap?
calls.reply: A map with a moving dot. The dot was on the hill school’s playing field. They were tracking him.
calls.note: Tessa Larkin saw the men by the bear trap tracking a dot on the hill school’s field.

women.name: Nadia Okafor
women.look: Dark skin, shoulder-length box braids, burgundy shirt and simple watch

own.label: Ask about forensic work
own.player: Is forensic work like the TV shows?
own.reply: No. Less glowing blue lights, more labelling bags. But I love it. Details don’t lie. People do.

own.label: Ask about her crosswords
own.player: I hear you do cryptic crosswords?
own.reply: In diners, with a pencil, like a woman from a better century. A good clue is a crime scene: everything you need is there, disguised.

own.label: Ask what’s bothering her at work
own.player: Something at work bothering you?
own.reply: The chain-of-custody log for the gala evidence has a gap. Two hours where nobody signed for the bag. Nobody else seems to care.
own.note: Nadia Okafor found a two-hour gap in the custody log for the gala evidence.

own.label: Ask what evidence can’t prove
own.player: What can’t evidence prove?
own.reply: Why. I can tell you who was in a room and when. I can’t tell you why anyone does anything. That’s what keeps me up.

own.label: Ask about her flat
own.player: What’s your place like?
own.reply: A window box of my grandmother’s roses and a shelf of crossword books from a better century. I do cryptics in the Lucky Cactus, in pencil. The waitress reads the clues over my shoulder and gets them first.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: Mum’s a pharmacist on the Sunfall Road. Dad was a hospital porter. He died of a stroke in the car park he’d parked in for twenty years. I check car parks now. It doesn’t help.

own.label: Ask what she’s waiting for
own.player: What are you waiting on at work?
own.reply: I’ve passed every exam the county offers. The promotion needs one sergeant’s signature, and it’s the wrong sergeant.

calls.label: Ask about the crossword clues
calls.player: You said the crossword talks to you?
calls.reply: Someone sets clues in the Daily that I’m certain are written for me. Last week: a nine-letter word for a trust on a ridge. I don’t know who. I’ve started leaving answers in the margins of the bar menus.
calls.note: Nadia Okafor believes someone is hiding clues for her in the Daily’s crossword.

calls.label: Ask what was in the evidence bag
calls.player: What went missing from the bag?
calls.reply: A torn ticket and a phone’s SIM. Two hours, nobody signs, and after it the bag is lighter. The SIM was Elena Cross’s. The last initials before the gap belong to a photographic assistant called Dale Pruett.
calls.note: Nadia Okafor says Elena Cross’s SIM card went missing from the evidence bag during a two-hour gap, after Dale Pruett last signed it.

women.name: Marianne Keene
women.look: Dark skin, layered caramel shoulder-length hair, tortoiseshell glasses, emerald wrap dress

own.label: Ask about keeping the foundation’s books
own.player: What’s it like keeping the foundation’s books?
own.reply: Twenty years of other people’s generosity in my neat handwriting. I know who gives, who boasts and who quietly takes it back.

own.label: Ask about her souvenirs
own.player: I hear you collect roadside souvenirs?
own.reply: A plastic flamingo from a motel that’s now a car park, a spoon from the world’s second-largest cactus. Junk with a memory. Better than diamonds without one.

own.label: Ask what she overheard
own.player: You look like you overheard something you shouldn’t have.
own.reply: Two board members arguing in the cloakroom on gala night over a sealed envelope. One said, It burns tonight or we all do. I was holding someone’s mink at the time.
own.note: Marianne Keene overheard two board members on gala night arguing over a sealed envelope that had to burn tonight.

own.label: Ask what forty taught her
own.player: What has forty taught you?
own.reply: That you stop performing for people who aren’t watching. And that a good coat is worth any price.

own.label: Ask how long she’s kept the books
own.player: How long have you done the books?
own.reply: Twenty years. Three treasurers, two chairwomen, and a filing system nobody else can read, which is deliberate. You don’t outlast people at the club by being easy to replace.

own.label: Ask if she’s ever been married
own.player: Were you ever married?
own.reply: Once, at twenty. He was going to manage the casino and managed to drink our house deposit instead. Divorced him at twenty-four. At the club that counts as taking holy orders.

own.label: Ask about her friend Ingrid
own.player: Did you have a best friend at the club?
own.reply: Ingrid Voss. Anna’s mother. She died in the cloakroom folding someone else’s wrap, and I held her hand. I’ve stood in that cloakroom every benefit since.

calls.label: Ask about the cloakroom safe
calls.player: Does the cloakroom have a safe?
calls.reply: It does. That afternoon I watched Elena Cross put a sealed envelope in it: pages in her own hand, copied from the real ledger. By morning the safe was empty. Two people have the combination. Me, and the events director.
calls.note: Marianne Keene saw Elena Cross put copied ledger pages in the cloakroom safe; only Marianne and Dorian Kell have the combination.

women.name: Leona Carlisle
women.look: Fair skin, chestnut curly bob, grey-green eyes, navy shift dress with pearls

own.label: Ask what compliance actually means
own.player: What does a compliance administrator actually do?
own.reply: I make sure rich people fill in their forms correctly. They hate me in a very polite way. I’m invited to everything and spoken to by no one.

own.label: Ask about her watercolours
own.player: What do you paint?
own.reply: The desert, over and over. It’s the only thing in Sunfall that doesn’t want anything from me. I’m bad at it, which is the point.

own.label: Ask about the most impulsive thing she’s done
own.player: What’s the most impulsive thing you’ve ever done?
own.reply: I bought a horse at a charity auction because the bidding went quiet and I felt sorry for it. The horse and the auctioneer. I visit him whenever I need someone who won’t ask about my portfolio.

own.label: Ask if she’s ever broken a rule
own.player: Have you ever broken a rule yourself?
own.reply: Once. I signed off a form I knew was wrong because a frightened woman asked me to. Best thing I’ve done in that job. Worst thing for my career.

own.label: Ask about her horse
own.player: Do you ride?
own.reply: I own a horse I can’t afford called Overdraft. The bidding went quiet at a charity auction and I felt sorry for him and the auctioneer. I visit him when I need someone who won’t ask about my portfolio.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What did your dad do?
own.reply: He drove for the Foundation for fifteen years and knew where every donor lived and which ones hit their wives. He died the year I finished college, and they gave me his job’s little sister. A desk.

own.label: Ask what the club thinks of her
own.player: What does the club make of you?
own.reply: I make rich people fill in forms. They hate me so politely it’s almost affection. Invited to everything, spoken to by no one.

calls.label: Ask about the form she signed
calls.player: What was the form you signed for Elena?
calls.reply: A transfer of the volunteer records to a new database, so nobody could change the list before the benefit. She was white as paper. The list on it still shows the original volunteers at the treasurer’s table, before the rota was overruled. It’s the only clean copy. I’ve never told my boss, because it would get her hurt and me merely fired.
calls.note: Leona Carlisle signed a form for Elena Cross that preserved the original Table 9 volunteer list before it was changed.

women.name: Elise Harrow
women.look: Warm brown skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, amber eyes, cream blazer over a silk camisole

own.label: Ask how she got the job
own.player: How did you end up keeping the foundation’s books?
own.reply: I was charming at the right party. Don’t look shocked. That’s how everyone here got their job; I’m just honest about it.

own.label: Ask about her singing
own.player: I heard you sing?
own.reply: In a little choir at St Brigid’s. I go for the music and stay because nobody there wants anything from me. Rare, in this town.

own.label: Ask what’s troubling her
own.player: Something’s bothering you. What is it?
own.reply: I have an invitation to a private dinner with my name on it. I don’t remember accepting it. Someone accepted it for me.
own.note: Elise Harrow has an invitation to a private dinner she never accepted.

own.label: Ask what she really wants
own.player: What do you really want, if you’re honest?
own.reply: To be someone people look at when I walk in. I know that’s shallow. Everyone wants it. I just say it out loud.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: The trailer park behind the drive-in, which is not a thing one says at the club. Mum cleaned the big houses on the reservoir side. I grew up seeing the inside of money through a door I was holding.

own.label: Ask about her flat
own.player: What’s your place like?
own.reply: A tiny flat above a nail bar, decorated with things borrowed from photo shoots and never returned. Everything I own looks expensive in one photo and nothing else.

own.label: Ask why she sings in a church choir
own.player: Why the choir at St Brigid’s?
own.reply: Old ladies who don’t know who my father is. Neither do I. It’s the only hour of the week where I’m not performing for somebody.

calls.label: Ask about the invitation
calls.player: Tell me about this invitation.
calls.reply: A heavy card, my name in a hand that isn’t mine. A private dinner at the lodge on the ridge, three nights from when it came, and the reply already filled in. Accepted. Somebody accepted for me. I’m thrilled and I’m scared, and I can’t tell which one is the point.
calls.note: Elise Harrow has an invitation to a private dinner at the lodge on Halcyon Ridge that someone else accepted in her name.

calls.label: Ask who’s catering the dinner
calls.player: Who’s catering this private dinner?
calls.reply: Late Service Catering, according to the accounts I keep. I have never once seen Late Service cater anything. Not a vol-au-vent.
calls.note: Elise Harrow says the lodge’s private dinner is booked to Late Service Catering, a firm she has never seen cater anything.

women.name: Francesca Quinn
women.look: Dark skin, brown waves with teal tips, a silver ear cuff, white linen trouser suit

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you actually do at the foundation?
own.reply: I make sure the rules are followed. Officially. Unofficially I make sure the right people know which rules exist.

own.label: Ask about her cookbooks
own.player: Someone said you collect cookbooks?
own.reply: Weird ones. A Victorian guide to dinner parties. A seventies one entirely about aspic. Every era thinks it has taste. Every era is wrong.

own.label: Ask what’s missing
own.player: Is something missing at work?
own.reply: One receipt. Gala night, a large cash withdrawal, signed off by someone who wasn’t there. I keep checking the drawer as if it’ll come back.
own.note: Francesca Quinn says a large cash withdrawal from gala night was signed off by someone who wasn’t there.

own.label: Ask what she cooks when she’s sad
own.player: What do you cook when you’re sad?
own.reply: My mother’s risotto. It takes forty minutes of stirring and you can’t leave it. It’s the only time I’m not thinking.

own.label: Ask what she actually does
own.player: What does compliance mean for the membership?
own.reply: Who’s nominated, who’s voted in, who is welcomed into the family. I know the by-laws better than the women who wrote them, and I use them like a scalpel.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Where’s your family from?
own.reply: Mum came from a village outside Naples to marry a Quinn with a bar in Old Town. The bar’s a vape shop now. Dad died when I was fifteen and Mum went home. She sends recipes instead of advice.

own.label: Ask what she’s climbing towards
own.player: What are you aiming for?
own.reply: The Foundation secretary’s post. I’ve realised lately it’s also a seat at a particular table. I haven’t decided if I want to sit there or set fire to it. Both appeal.

calls.label: Ask who could have signed it
calls.player: Who signed for the cash that night?
calls.reply: Hugh Beaumont’s name, in a hand that isn’t his. There’s a woman at the club who can do anyone’s handwriting after an hour with a sample. Delphine Moreau. And the sum is exactly what a party girl was paid to keep one room off the after-party list.
calls.note: Francesca Quinn says the missing receipt was signed in Hugh Beaumont’s name by Delphine Moreau, who can forge any hand.

women.name: Naomi Whitlock
women.look: Medium-brown skin, natural afro puff, a tiny scar through one eyebrow, tailored grey waistcoat and slacks

own.label: Ask what a charity’s books reveal
own.player: What do you see, keeping a charity’s books?
own.reply: Every receipt tells a story. Most of them say lunch. A worrying number say lunch for twelve.

own.label: Ask about ballroom dancing
own.player: How’s the ballroom dancing going?
own.reply: My instructor says I lead with my head. I keep counting. Apparently you’re meant to feel it. I’ve never felt anything I didn’t first put in a spreadsheet.

own.label: Ask what it’s like being the youngest at the club
own.player: Is it strange being the youngest one at the club?
own.reply: Everyone calls me sweetheart and then asks me to fix their phone. I’ve set up the same woman’s email four times. She sends me fruit baskets.

own.label: Ask what she’s overthinking right now
own.player: What are you overthinking right now?
own.reply: Whether I replied too fast. Whether that sounded keen. Whether this sentence is too long. It is, isn’t it.

own.label: Ask about the ranch
own.player: Tell me about the ranch.
own.reply: Five generations past the canyon. My grandfather keeps saying no to developers. The developers keep coming back with different names on the same letterhead.

own.label: Ask why she learns ballroom
own.player: Why ballroom dancing?
own.reply: My instructor says I lead with my head. I keep counting. I’ve never felt anything I didn’t first put in a spreadsheet.

own.label: Ask if people are nice to her
own.player: Is everyone kind to you at the club?
own.reply: Very. Suspiciously. One lady has asked me twice whether I have a young man. I think she’s interested in the ranch. It comes with me, you see. That’s the whole family joke.

calls.label: Ask about the lunch receipts
calls.player: What did you find in the receipts?
calls.reply: The lunch-for-twelve ones are all signed with the same two initials, and every date matches the committee’s private dinners. I made a spreadsheet. A spreadsheet is how I have feelings.
calls.note: Naomi Whitlock says the Foundation’s lunch-for-twelve receipts match the dates of the committee’s private dinners.

women.name: Bianca Roth
women.look: Olive skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, a tiny scar through one eyebrow, white linen trouser suit

own.label: Ask about her job at the foundation
own.player: What does a compliance administrator do all day?
own.reply: I make sure the right forms exist so that, if anyone ever asks, the right forms exist. It’s theatre, darling, with staples.

own.label: Ask about repairing watches
own.player: You repair watches?
own.reply: Old ones. Wind-up, no batteries, nothing that talks to your phone. A watch that keeps time without being told to is the most honest thing in this town.

own.label: Ask what she overheard
own.player: You look like you overheard something.
own.reply: Gala night, the back corridor: two board members arguing over a sealed envelope that had to be gone by morning. One of them saw me. Neither of them has looked at me since.
own.note: Bianca Roth heard two board members on gala night arguing over a sealed envelope that had to be gone by morning.

own.label: Ask why old watches matter to her
own.player: Why do old watches matter to you?
own.reply: Because someone made them to last a lifetime and they did. Name one thing you own that was built to outlive you.

own.label: Ask about her husband
own.player: Are you married?
own.reply: To my first boyfriend, Gil. He’s a reservoir engineer. The committee offered to nominate him three times and I said no, pleasantly, as a joke, three times. We are uneventfully happy. At the club that’s practically a scandal.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: Above my dad’s pharmacy in Old Town. I learned to read the labels before the newspapers. A label is a promise somebody can be sued for.

own.label: Ask what she remembers
own.player: What do you remember about people?
own.reply: Everyone brings me their form and their birthday. I remember both. People think those are the same thing.

calls.label: Ask what she signed four years ago
calls.player: What did you sign that bothers you?
calls.reply: The trust on the ridge. Its donor registration has my signature on it. I knew what it was the day it came across my desk, and I know now. The original is in the back of a watch case, because nobody looks inside a watch.
calls.note: Bianca Roth signed the Halcyon Ridge Trust’s registration knowing it was a shell, and has kept the original.

women.name: Simone Ellery
women.look: Light-brown skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, a beauty mark above her lip, navy shift dress with pearls

women.name: Adeline Marsh
women.look: Tall and very slender, porcelain skin, a sharp aquiline nose, deep-set dark eyes with a cool sullen stare, a slim small-busted model figure, long red curls, a gold-buttoned navy blazer

women.name: Valerie Huxley
women.look: Rail-thin runway-model frame, a slim small-busted figure, translucent pale skin, high cheekbones, cool dark sullen eyes with faint shadows beneath, honey-blonde hair scraped back, a pale pink slip-style sheath dress

own.label: Ask about her balcony garden
own.player: What are you growing on that balcony?
own.reply: Basil, mint and a rosemary bush with ambitions. The mint is trying to take over. Honestly, I respect it.

own.label: Ask what she notices at the club
own.player: What do you notice that nobody else does at the club?
own.reply: Who pays, and who reaches for their wallet slowly. You could run the whole town’s gossip off that one detail.

own.label: Ask if numbers ever lie
own.player: Do numbers ever lie?
own.reply: Never. People lie with them all the time. I just put the numbers next to each other and wait.

own.label: Ask if she wants a different life
own.player: Do you ever want a completely different life?
own.reply: I want a small one. A kitchen with herbs on the sill and someone who comes home when he says he will. Everyone at the club wants more. I want enough.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A studio above a shuttered bookshop in Old Town. I read on the balcony until the light goes. I eat little and sleep badly, but the rosemary is thriving.

own.label: Ask about the Huxleys
own.player: Is Huxley an old Sunfall name?
own.reply: My grandfather sat on the Foundation’s first board and lost everything in the casino’s first year. We were somebody once. Now I keep the books for the people who used to visit us.

own.label: Ask what she wants
own.player: What do you actually want?
own.reply: A kitchen with herbs on the sill and a man who comes home when he says he will. That isn’t small. It’s just quiet.

calls.label: Ask about her scholarship
calls.player: How did you get your scholarship?
calls.reply: Approved by the treasurer himself, outside the usual round, the same month something that happened to me in a hotel was settled by a solicitor I never met. I put my award next to the trust’s payments. The dates match. I don’t know yet if I’m evidence or a receipt.
calls.note: Valerie Huxley’s scholarship was approved by Augustus Pell outside the normal round, in the same month as the trust’s payments.

women.name: Ruth Calder
women.look: Dark skin, short silver-dyed crop, rosy cheeks, powder-blue twinset

own.label: Ask about her twinsets
own.player: Do you really own that many twinsets?
own.reply: Eleven. In eleven shades of blue. My mother says a woman should always look as if she’s about to be photographed. Nobody has ever photographed me.

own.label: Ask about her pottery
own.player: How’s the pottery going?
own.reply: I made a vase for the club raffle and someone used it as an ashtray. I was so proud. It was being used.

own.label: Ask about her most awkward moment
own.player: What’s the most awkward thing you’ve ever done?
own.reply: I curtsied to the mayor. He’s a dentist. He was very kind about it, which made it worse.

own.label: Ask who her rival is
own.player: Is it true you have a rival at the club?
own.reply: Everyone has one. Mine wears red to annoy me. The terrible secret is that I like her, and I think she knows.

own.label: Ask what she does
own.player: What do you look after at the Foundation?
own.reply: Every grant: scholarships, the food programme, the museum money. I read every application and I remember every one. People think that makes me kind. It makes me tired.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: What was your mother like?
own.reply: Railway family, married up, spent thirty years making sure nobody noticed the join. She taught me twinsets and silence. I kept the twinsets.

own.label: Ask if she has family nearby
own.player: Any family in Sunfall?
own.reply: A niece in the Old Quarter. Black lipstick, terrible friends, a heart like a lighthouse. I raised her. She’s the one person in the world I would do anything for, and I mean anything.

calls.label: Ask what’s frightening her
calls.player: You sound frightened. What’s happened?
calls.reply: Someone is using my name. Three young women have had messages, signed Ruth Calder, saying their grants are approved pending a private meeting at the lodge. I sent none of them. One wrote to thank me. I know what my name is being used to do, and I don’t know who to tell who doesn’t already know.
calls.note: Ruth Calder says messages signed with her name are inviting young grant applicants to private meetings at the lodge.

women.name: Serena Bellweather
women.look: Light olive skin, cornrows into a low bun, thin wire-rimmed glasses, cream blazer over a silk camisole

women.name: Helena Forsyth
women.look: Dark skin, dark French braid, a small nose stud, powder-blue twinset

women.name: Cecilia Prado

women.name: Brielle Kenton

women.name: Carmen Bellini

women.name: Penelope Kline

women.name: Irene Valencia
women.look: Freckled fair skin, rose-gold bob, freckles across her nose, gold-buttoned navy blazer

women.name: Whitney Ashford

women.name: Delphine Moreau
women.look: Rosy fair skin, copper waist-length waves, strong dark brows, powder-blue twinset

women.name: Catalina Reyes
women.look: Deep brown skin, rose-gold bob, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, white linen trouser suit

women.name: Danica Holt
women.look: Deep brown skin, golden-brown ringlets, a silver ear cuff, windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask about photographing crime scenes
own.player: What’s it like photographing crime scenes?
own.reply: You learn to look at the worst day of someone’s life as a problem of light. Then you go home and look at nothing for an hour.

own.label: Ask about the watches
own.player: You repair watches?
own.reply: Badly, slowly, happily. A watch is a crime scene in reverse: every part tells you exactly what happened, if you’re patient.

own.label: Ask what’s missing at work
own.player: Something missing at work?
own.reply: The key to the filing cabinet with the gala photographs. It was there, then it wasn’t, and the sign-out sheet is blank. Somebody in our own building wanted those prints.
own.note: Danica Holt says the key to the cabinet holding the gala crime-scene photographs went missing inside the police station.

own.label: Ask what colour she sees most at work
own.player: What colour do you see most at work?
own.reply: Beige. Carpets, walls, coats. The worst things happen in the most boring rooms.

own.label: Ask how she started so young
own.player: How did you get the job at seventeen?
own.reply: I photographed the drive-in’s back field every dawn for a year, where my cousin Dana was found. I sent the station the photos. They hired me. I think they didn’t know what else to do with me.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: At my aunt’s, Dana’s mum’s. It’s a house of grief, and I’ve decided to be the light in it. Some days I’m a very small light.

own.label: Ask what she notices at scenes
own.player: What do you notice first at a scene?
own.reply: Beige. Carpets, walls, coats. The worst things happen in the most boring rooms. I bring a red scarf to every scene, just to see one colour.

calls.label: Ask about her practice photos
calls.player: Did you take any photos of your own that night?
calls.reply: Practice frames, of the club’s kitchen door. I wasn’t meant to. They show a grey car with its door open and a shape in the back seat. I haven’t told Katrina. I don’t know who I’d be telling after her.
calls.note: Danica Holt’s practice photos from the gala show a grey car at the club’s kitchen door with a shape in the back seat.

women.name: Sasha Mahoney
women.look: Olive skin, natural afro puff, deep dimples, windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask what the numbers say about Sunfall
own.player: What do the numbers say about Sunfall?
own.reply: Most accidents happen in the kitchen. Statistically, your toaster is a bigger threat than any stranger. Sleep well.

own.label: Ask about her book club
own.player: What’s your book club reading?
own.reply: Officially, a serious novel about grief. Actually, we drink wine and talk about our exes. Nobody has finished a book since we started.

own.label: Ask how a statistician can be impulsive
own.player: How is a statistician impulsive?
own.reply: I know the odds, so I ignore them. Knowing a thing is unlikely just makes me want to see it happen.

own.label: Ask which number she can’t forget
own.player: Is there a number you can’t forget?
own.reply: Seventeen. The number of calls a woman made before anyone came. I built a model so it would never happen again. It still happens.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Who taught you numbers?
own.reply: Mum teaches maths at the high school and taught me to count cards at family poker. Dad runs the boat hire on the reservoir. Between them, I don’t trust water or luck.

own.label: Ask what actually kills people
own.player: What’s actually dangerous in Sunfall?
own.reply: Your kitchen. Most accidents happen there. Then ladders. Then the reservoir at the regatta. Strangers come a long way down the list, which nobody wants to hear.

calls.label: Ask about the seventeen calls
calls.player: Why did nobody come for seventeen calls?
calls.reply: The nearest patrol car was on a private job: escorting a Foundation vehicle up to the ridge, signed off by Sergeant Lowry. I found it in the data my first year. They told me it was a coding error. I kept the raw log.
calls.note: Sasha Mahoney says the patrol car that never came was escorting a Foundation vehicle to the ridge on Sergeant Lowry’s orders.

calls.label: Ask about her dad and the regatta
calls.player: Did your dad ever see anything at the reservoir?
calls.reply: He gave a statement once, years ago. A man called Ellis Dane drowned at a club regatta. Dad said Dane was sober and the boat had been tampered with. The case was closed as misadventure. Dad hasn’t hired a boat to the club since.
calls.note: Sasha Mahoney’s father says Ellis Dane, who drowned at a club regatta, was sober and his boat had been tampered with.

women.name: Imani Harper
women.look: Pale skin, layered caramel shoulder-length hair, freckles across her nose, windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask about the evidence archive
own.player: What’s the evidence archive like?
own.reply: Rows of boxes holding the worst days of people’s lives, sorted by number. I label them carefully. It feels like the least I can do.

own.label: Ask about her cactus garden
own.player: I heard you keep cacti indoors?
own.reply: Thirty-one of them. They’re the only things in Sunfall that thrive on neglect, and I respect that.

own.label: Ask what’s weighing on her
own.player: You seem like something’s weighing on you.
own.reply: I promised my mum I’d go home to Atlanta by now. I keep not going. Sunfall gets its hooks in you.

own.label: Ask about the box nobody opens
own.player: Is there a box in the archive nobody opens?
own.reply: Shelf nine, bottom row. It’s labelled with a case number that doesn’t exist. I’ve never opened it. I think about it every day.

own.label: Ask where she’s from
own.player: You’re not from here, are you?
own.reply: Atlanta. I promised my mum I’d come home after a year. That was two years ago. She’s a hospital administrator and wanted me to be a lawyer. I label boxes. We’re both disappointed in very organised ways.

own.label: Ask who cuts her hair
own.player: Who cuts your hair?
own.reply: Me, in the bathroom, with the good scissors. Freckles I’ve stopped hiding, windbreaker for the archive cold. I’m very low maintenance. The cacti are high maintenance about being ignored.

calls.label: Ask what’s strange about the box
calls.player: What’s strange about that box?
calls.reply: There’s no such case. I checked. And somebody dusts that box every week, and it isn’t me. My boss says it’s an old filing error. Filing errors don’t get dusted.
calls.note: Imani Harper says the evidence box on shelf nine has no real case number and someone dusts it every week.

women.name: Leila Sayeed
women.look: Olive skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, hazel eyes, plain white shirt and slim black trousers

own.label: Ask what a custody nurse does
own.player: What does a custody nurse actually do?
own.reply: I patch up people on the worst night of their lives, usually at both ends of the handcuffs. Everyone is polite to the nurse. Even the ones who bite.

own.label: Ask where she wants to be in ten years
own.player: Where do you want to be in ten years?
own.reply: Running the whole place. Or a little clinic by the sea. I change my mind every shift. Ambition is just restlessness with a plan.

own.label: Ask what she grows on her balcony
own.player: What are you growing out there?
own.reply: Mint for tea and chillies for revenge. Lavender too, for the nights I come home smelling of the station.

own.label: Ask what scares her at work
own.player: Does anything at work scare you?
own.reply: The quiet ones. The ones who say they’re fine and look at the wall. I’ve learned to sit with them a bit longer.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: They run a chemist on the Sunfall Road, two doors from Nadia Okafor’s mum’s. The mothers are best friends and sworn enemies. Their window displays are a cold war.

own.label: Ask how she stays so neat
own.player: How do you stay that tidy in custody?
own.reply: I change my shirt twice a shift. Some nights three times. Clean white is a kindness to the next person. They’re having a bad enough night.

calls.label: Ask about the quiet girl
calls.player: Who was the quiet one you sat with?
calls.reply: A graduate student held overnight after a protest. She looked at the wall for an hour and said one thing: that she knew about the car and didn’t know how to stop it. Her name was Rosa Gutierrez. The custody sergeant was listening at the door, so I wrote nothing down.
calls.note: Leila Sayeed says Rosa Gutierrez, held overnight after a protest, said she knew about the car and didn’t know how to stop it.

women.name: Joanne Kendrick
women.look: Freckled fair skin, natural afro puff, thin wire-rimmed glasses, maroon fleece and jeans

own.label: Ask what dispatch is like
own.player: What’s it like being a dispatcher?
own.reply: People ring me on the worst day of their lives and I have to sound calm. Then I hang up and shake. Then the next one rings.

own.label: Ask about her pottery
own.player: How’s the pottery going?
own.reply: I’ve made eleven bowls and none of them are round. My mum uses them anyway. She says they have character. They have holes.

own.label: Ask about the strangest call she’s taken
own.player: What’s the strangest call you’ve ever taken?
own.reply: A man who wanted us to arrest the moon because it was too bright. I logged it. Politely. You never know.

own.label: Ask how she switches off after a shift
own.player: How do you switch off after a shift?
own.reply: I don’t, really. I lie awake wondering how they all got on. You never find out. That’s the worst part.

own.label: Ask about Doreen
own.player: What’s Doreen like to work for?
own.reply: Twenty-two years on the phones and she’s heard everything twice. She taught me to sound calm. She didn’t teach me how to stop shaking after. I don’t think she has.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Is it just you and your mum?
own.reply: Dad was a guard on the last passenger train out of Sunfall. He’s gone now. Mum cleans at the museum. She uses my bowls even though they leak. She says they have character.

calls.label: Ask about the call she can’t forget
calls.player: Is there a call you can’t get out of your head?
calls.reply: A woman, out of breath, on a payphone at the weigh station by the old junction. Someone was coming. I put her through to patrol. Patrol was on a private escort. Doreen said log it as a prank. I did. I hear her when I close my eyes.
calls.note: Joanne Kendrick took a payphone call from a frightened woman at the old junction’s weigh station on gala night, logged as a prank.

calls.label: Ask if she’s noticed anything at the station
calls.player: Seen anything odd at the station?
calls.reply: The lad from the motor pool keeps washing the grey sedan. Every day. Nobody washes a police car every day. Not here.
calls.note: Joanne Kendrick says a station mechanic keeps washing the grey sedan every day.

women.name: Cassidy Boone
women.look: Fair skin, short silver-dyed crop, amber eyes, denim shirt with rolled sleeves

own.label: Ask what the records room is like
own.player: What’s it like down in the records room?
own.reply: Quiet. Dusty. Every file is somebody’s worst week, filed alphabetically. I like it down there. Paper doesn’t lie to you.

own.label: Ask about her sketches
own.player: What do you sketch?
own.reply: Old shopfronts before they’re knocked down. The barber’s, the cobbler’s, the old cinema. Somebody should remember what this town looked like.

own.label: Ask what loyalty means to her
own.player: What does loyalty mean to you?
own.reply: Turning up. Twice, if needed. Most people say they’d help you move house. I actually own a van.

own.label: Ask if a file ever stayed with her
own.player: Has a file ever stayed with you?
own.reply: One. An old case nobody closed. I read it every few weeks. Someone ought to keep looking, even if it’s only me.

own.label: Ask if she’s good at helping people move
own.player: Are you the friend with the van?
own.reply: I am the friend with the van, and I actually turn up. That’s rarer than it should be. Bring biscuits and lift the heavy end.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Where are the Boones from?
own.reply: Up in the hills. Logging, until the logging went. Dad repairs chainsaws and says about nine words a day. Mum left for a preacher when I was eleven. Dad and I are fine. Quiet, but fine.

calls.label: Ask about the case she rereads
calls.player: Which old case do you keep rereading?
calls.reply: Ellis Dane, fourteen years ago. Married a Bluebird. Drowned at a club regatta. A witness said he was sober and the boat was tampered with. Closed as misadventure by a young detective constable called Vic Lowry. I read it every few weeks.
calls.note: Cassidy Boone says the Ellis Dane drowning was closed as misadventure by Vic Lowry when he was a young detective.

calls.label: Ask what her pull cards show
calls.player: Who’s been pulling files lately?
calls.reply: I keep the stubs of every file pulled and by whom. Lately the stubs say a sergeant took the sign-out sheet for the gala cabinet the week a man vanished, and the sheet that came back was blank.
calls.note: Cassidy Boone’s records show Sergeant Lowry pulled the gala cabinet’s sign-out sheet, which came back blank.

women.name: Naoko Watanabe
women.look: Light-brown skin, blunt black bob, rosy cheeks, windbreaker over a sports top

women.name: Brenda Velasco
women.look: Lean and wiry, golden-tan skin, high sharp cheekbones, hooded dark eyes, a strong nose, a chestnut high ponytail, thin wire-rimmed glasses, an olive field jacket

own.label: Ask what a collision investigator does
own.player: What does a collision investigator actually do?
own.reply: I measure skid marks and work out who’s lying. Everyone says the other car came out of nowhere. Nothing comes out of nowhere.

own.label: Ask about her rescue dog
own.player: Tell me about your dog.
own.reply: Biscuit. He’s fourteen, half blind and convinced the postman is the devil. He sleeps on my feet. I’d die for him.

own.label: Ask what she’s most sceptical about
own.player: What are you most sceptical about?
own.reply: Men who say they’re great drivers. Every single one. I have the photographs.

own.label: Ask if the job changed how she drives
own.player: Has the job changed how you drive?
own.reply: I drive like my grandmother now. I hold my breath at every junction. I’ve seen what a second does.

own.label: Ask about her dad
own.player: How did you end up in collisions?
own.reply: Dad ran the breakdown truck in the canyon for thirty years. He pulled every wreck off that road. I used to ride along. You learn to read a road from the tow hook end.

own.label: Ask what she’s like off duty
own.player: What are you like when you’re not measuring skid marks?
own.reply: Exactly the same, but in slippers. Biscuit sleeps on my feet and growls at the postman, and I drink tea out of a mug that says world’s okayest driver.

calls.label: Ask about Paul Sanderson’s crash
calls.player: What was wrong with the crash at the old junction?
calls.reply: No skid marks. A man brakes when he’s about to die. Paul Sanderson didn’t, or couldn’t. There was a second set of tyre tracks. I said so and was moved off the case. Four crashes at that junction in nine years. All Foundation men. All weather.
calls.note: Brenda Velasco says the four crashes at the old junction, all Foundation men, had no skid marks and a second set of tyre tracks.

calls.label: Ask what she found at the weigh station
calls.player: Did you find anything at the weigh station?
calls.reply: Fresh tracks in the yard, a grey sedan’s, beside a window with blood on the frame. I photographed the window. The photo’s in Markham’s drawer.
calls.note: Brenda Velasco found grey sedan tracks and blood on a window frame at the old junction’s weigh station.

women.name: Alisha Benton
women.look: Lean and athletic, olive skin, a slightly crooked nose from an old break, intense dark eyes, honey-blonde beach waves, a windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask if forensics is like on television
own.player: Is forensic work like it is on television?
own.reply: On television it takes an afternoon and a dramatic zoom. Here it takes a fortnight and a form. Nobody has ever said enhance to me.

own.label: Ask about her old cameras
own.player: What’s the appeal of old film cameras?
own.reply: You only get thirty-six chances, so you have to mean it. Phones turned everyone into people who take a thousand pictures of nothing.

own.label: Ask what she notices about people first
own.player: What do you notice about people first?
own.reply: Their hands. Bitten nails, paint, rings they keep turning. Hands tell you what faces are trained to hide.

own.label: Ask if there’s a film she’s never developed
own.player: Is there a roll of film you’ve never developed?
own.reply: One. My dad’s last roll. I’m scared it’s just the garden. I’m more scared it isn’t.

own.label: Ask where she develops film
own.player: Where do you develop your film?
own.reply: My bathroom’s a darkroom. My towels are a tragedy. Every camera on my shelf was dead when I found it. I like bringing things back.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Who taught you about cameras?
own.reply: Dad. Ray Benton, wedding photographer, the kindest man in the county. He died of a heart attack in the club’s garden, mid-wedding, with a roll in the camera. The club sent flowers.

own.label: Ask about her nose
own.player: How did you break your nose?
own.reply: Sparring. A fitness instructor called Lauren broke it and then cried more than I did. I kept the bend. It’s my favourite thing about my face now.

calls.label: Ask what the fire chemistry said
calls.player: What did the lab say about Vale’s fire?
calls.reply: Set by somebody who knew nothing about fire, with something bought at a garden centre. Amateurs leave a lot of chemistry. Whoever it was burned their hands, I’d bet my best camera.
calls.note: Alisha Benton says Vale’s fire was set by an amateur using garden-centre accelerant, who probably burned their hands.

calls.label: Ask who asked about the lab’s negatives
calls.player: Has anyone been asking about the lab?
calls.reply: A woman from the club, Genevieve Locke, twice, very lightly, whether we keep negatives of what we process. Nobody asks that lightly twice.
calls.note: Alisha Benton says Genevieve Locke has twice asked whether the police lab keeps negatives.
