women.name: Adriana Ponce
women.look: Golden-tan skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, a beauty mark above her lip, overalls and a bandana

own.label: Ask why she campaigns
own.player: Why climate campaigning?
own.reply: Because my town in Sonora ran out of water when I was twelve. People argue about models. I remember the taps.

own.label: Ask about her football
own.player: Five-a-side, I heard?
own.reply: Every week with women half my age. I’m slower and dirtier. They’re learning a lot.

own.label: Ask what she makes of the young activists
own.player: What do you make of the younger activists?
own.reply: They’re brave and they’re online. They mistake a hashtag for a hard week’s work. I tell them: knock on doors, or go home. They hate me. They come back.

own.label: Ask what she got wrong when she was young
own.player: What did you get wrong when you were young?
own.reply: I thought shouting was the same as winning. It isn’t. The people I changed were the ones I had a coffee with.

own.label: Ask about the photographs on her wall
own.player: What are all the photos on your wall?
own.reply: Towns that ran out of water. Mine is the first one, top left. A river sold upstream when I was twelve. My family came north the year the taps stopped.

own.label: Ask about her parents
own.player: What did your parents do here?
own.reply: Dad was a mechanic who became a janitor. Mum cleaned houses and sang while she did it. I learned organising from watching her get six rich houses to pay on time.

calls.label: Ask about the torn page in the journal
calls.player: What was on the page torn out of the journal?
calls.reply: The night before we voted to join the protest, someone wrote in the shared journal: three names and a car park bay number. Vanessa’s hand. The next morning the page was gone. I read it before it went.
calls.note: Adriana Ponce read a torn-out journal page in Vanessa Greer’s hand listing three names and a car park bay.

women.name: Sienna Navarro
women.look: Olive skin, burgundy-dyed curls, grey-green eyes, embroidered peasant blouse

own.label: Ask what she’s organising
own.player: What are you organising at the moment?
own.reply: A mural on the underpass. Forty volunteers, three committees and one argument about whether a cactus is problematic. It’s a cactus.

own.label: Ask about the drums
own.player: How are the drums going?
own.reply: Loudly. My neighbour bangs on the wall in time now. I think we’re a band.

own.label: Ask what she overthinks most
own.player: What do you overthink the most?
own.reply: Group chats. If I put a full stop, am I angry? If I don’t, am I unserious? I once drafted a thumbs-up for ten minutes.

own.label: Ask if she ever tires of causes
own.player: Do you ever get tired of causes?
own.reply: All the time. Some days I just want to paint something pretty that doesn’t mean anything. I’m not allowed to say that at meetings.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: Dad painted houses and Mum sold them. That’s the whole economy in one marriage. I paint walls nobody can sell. I think that’s growth.

own.label: Ask how she got into organising
own.player: How did you end up organising?
own.reply: I was a shy art student. Organising turned out to be a way of being in a room without anyone looking at me. Everyone looks at the clipboard.

calls.label: Ask about the crescent on the mural
calls.player: Why is there a crescent moon on the underpass mural?
calls.reply: A volunteer added it and we voted to keep it, for the desert nights. Then Hana Park told me that crescent is a design somebody paid cash for, and it’s on a flyer for something called the Midnight Rite. The volunteer was a girl called Sorrel, and she paints the night sky like she’s been told where the stars go.
calls.note: Sienna Navarro says the mural’s crescent was added by Sorrel Vane, and the same design is on the Midnight Rite flyer.

women.name: Nora Hadley
women.look: Warm brown skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, a silver ear cuff, vintage windbreaker

own.label: Ask what her heresy is
own.player: What’s an opinion your friends hate?
own.reply: That nuclear power is the best thing for the climate. Say that in our group chat and watch people combust. Ironically.

own.label: Ask about learning Italian
own.player: You’re learning Italian?
own.reply: Badly. I want to read Dante in the original before I die. Ambitious, for someone who still says grazie wrong.

own.label: Ask what’s bothering her
own.player: Something on your mind?
own.reply: A woman from our march saw something on gala night. She told me, then a week later she told the police the exact opposite. Someone got to her.
own.note: Nora Hadley says a witness changed her story about gala night after someone got to her.

own.label: Ask what she believes that her friends don’t
own.player: What do you believe that your friends don’t?
own.reply: That men and women want different things, mostly, and that’s fine. Saying it at a meeting is like admitting you eat meat.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What does your dad do?
own.reply: He’s a surveyor. He surveyed the ridge road once and said it was fine. Mum’s a school nurse. I’m the nobody in particular they made, with opinions.

own.label: Ask what she reads
own.player: What are you reading?
own.reply: Italian grammar, badly, and everything in the library by people who were wrong in public and survived it. I’d like to be wrong in public one day. Properly.

calls.label: Ask about her father’s survey
calls.player: Is something wrong with your dad’s survey?
calls.reply: He said the ridge road was fine. It isn’t fine. Lorries go up it at night that the survey says can’t. I think somebody paid him to say so, and I think he knows I think it.
calls.note: Nora Hadley suspects her father was paid to sign off the ridge road as safe.

women.name: Daisy Chen
women.look: Dark skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, tortoiseshell glasses, hand-knitted jumper

own.label: Ask what she makes her collages from
own.player: What do you make the collages from?
own.reply: Old magazines, bus tickets, receipts people drop. I like turning things people threw away into something they’d stop to look at.

own.label: Ask why she’s bad at small talk
own.player: Why are you so bad at small talk?
own.reply: Because I’d rather know what you’re afraid of than what the weather is doing. It makes me very bad at parties and very good at funerals.

own.label: Ask about the worst crisis she’s handled
own.player: What’s the worst crisis you’ve handled?
own.reply: A pensioners’ craft fair where the glue gun caught fire. I put it out with a tea towel and nobody stopped knitting. Best day of my career.

own.label: Ask what she’s like when nobody’s watching
own.player: What are you like when nobody’s watching?
own.reply: Sillier. I dance in the kitchen and talk back to the radio. Most people only ever meet the organiser.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you have family here?
own.reply: My sister Mei, downstairs. She does hair and hears everything. I make art and say nothing. Between us we know the whole street.

own.label: Ask about her parents
own.player: What happened to your parents?
own.reply: Dad ran a restaurant and died in it. Mum sold it and went to the coast. Mei and I stayed, which nobody expected, least of all us.

calls.label: Ask what odd thing she’s picked up lately
calls.player: Found anything odd for your collages?
calls.reply: A garden centre receipt dropped on campus, for a quantity of something nobody gardens with. I glued it into a piece called Sunfall. Nobody’s read it yet. Somebody will.
calls.note: Daisy Chen found a garden-centre receipt on campus for a quantity of something nobody gardens with.

women.name: Zoe Whitaker
women.look: Light-brown skin, golden-brown ringlets, freckles across her nose, oversized thrifted cardigan

women.name: Khadija Rahman
women.look: Warm brown skin, cornrows into a low bun, strong dark brows, embroidered peasant blouse

own.label: Ask about her film nights
own.player: What do you show at the film nights?
own.reply: Old comedies, mostly. I tried a serious documentary once. Twelve people came and one of them was asleep. Now it’s slapstick and popcorn and the hall is full.

own.label: Ask what community meetings are really like
own.player: What are community meetings really like?
own.reply: Two hours, three people talking and a biscuit tin nobody opens until the end. The biscuits are the only thing everyone agrees on.

own.label: Ask what she disagrees with her friends about
own.player: What do you disagree with your friends about?
own.reply: Quite a lot, quietly. They think everything is a system. I think a lot of things are just people being rude. You can’t fix rude with a workshop.

own.label: Ask what she misses most
own.player: What do you miss most?
own.reply: My grandmother’s kitchen. Everyone shouting and nobody angry. Sunfall is very polite. I miss being shouted at with love.

own.label: Ask how she runs film night
own.player: Where do you get a projector?
own.reply: I share one with Gwen, who runs a yard film night on alternate weeks. It travels between us in a shopping trolley. It has seen things.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What does your family do?
own.reply: Mum runs a pharmacy on the Sunfall Road and has a strong view on everything. Dad died when I was twenty. In our house you were shouted at with love or not at all.

calls.label: Ask what went wrong at film night
calls.player: What happened at the film night you stopped?
calls.reply: Four minutes of film that wasn’t mine came up between reels. A room with candles, a circle of people, and a bell. I said it was a fault. It came in the shared projector from Gwen’s yard night. A man asked her to show it as a favour. Brad Keller. The reel is in my flat. I don’t want it there.
calls.note: Khadija Rahman has a reel showing a candlelit circle and a bell, passed on by Brad Keller.

women.name: Esther Yu
women.look: Medium-brown skin, glossy black ponytail, a silver ear cuff, oversized thrifted cardigan

women.name: Cassandra Finch
women.look: Bird-like and slight, warm brown skin, cropped bleached hair, enormous dark tired eyes with a sullen look, a small gap between her front teeth, a slim small-busted figure, a linen shirt and a canvas tote

own.label: Ask how she stays so cheerful
own.player: How do you stay so cheerful?
own.reply: Stubbornness. I decided to be cheerful years ago and I refuse to back down now. Out of spite, mainly.

own.label: Ask what she paints
own.player: What do you paint?
own.reply: Skies. Sunfall has the best skies in the world and everyone is looking at their phones under them. Sorry. Not you. Well, a bit you.

own.label: Ask if she fits in with her group
own.player: Do you fit in with the others?
own.reply: Not really. I go to the meetings, bring the cake and vote how I like. They keep me for the cake.

own.label: Ask what she’ll never give up on
own.player: What will you never give up on?
own.reply: People. Even the awful ones. Especially the awful ones. Someone gave up on me once, and it took years to undo.

own.label: Ask where she paints
own.player: Where do you paint?
own.reply: On the roof above the Sisters’ charity shop. I rent the room underneath from Lucia. Best sky in Sunfall and nobody up there but me and the pigeons.

own.label: Ask about growing up
own.player: What were you like as a teenager?
own.reply: Ill, mostly. Thin and tired with a thing the doctors were slow to name. Mum left. Dad sold farm machinery and sat with me. I decided to be cheerful out of spite and I’ve never backed down.

calls.label: Ask about her neighbour
calls.player: Who lives next door to you?
calls.reply: Nobody, for two years. Now the light comes on behind the blind at night and goes off before dawn. Lucia takes two lunches up the stairs. Through the wall I heard a woman crying, and once, laughing. I painted the blind with the light behind it. I won’t say more.
calls.note: Cassandra Finch says someone has been living secretly in the flat next to hers, above the Sisters’ charity shop.

calls.label: Ask what she kept from a meeting
calls.player: Did you keep anything from the group’s meetings?
calls.reply: Vanessa Greer’s cup. She left it, and I don’t give up on anyone. There’s a crescent painted on the bottom. I’m trying to decide if that means anything.
calls.note: Cassandra Finch kept a cup Vanessa Greer left behind, with a crescent on the base.

women.name: Eden Sutherland
women.look: Waifish and slight, a slim small-busted figure, light-brown skin, freckles across her nose, huge dark sleepy eyes with a sullen stare, buzz-cut dark hair, a gap-toothed smile, overalls and a bandana

own.label: Ask what campaigning is like day to day
own.player: What’s campaigning actually like day to day?
own.reply: Leaflets, rain and men in big cars telling me to get a job. This is my job. It pays less than their car.

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: You sing in a choir?
own.reply: Alto. Church hall, old ladies, hymns I don’t believe in. It’s the only place I feel calm. Don’t tell my friends.

own.label: Ask why she’s so blunt
own.player: Why are you so blunt?
own.reply: Because the world’s on fire and I haven’t got time to be nice about it. I’m nice afterwards. I bring soup.

own.label: Ask what she gives away
own.player: What do you give away?
own.reply: Most of my wages, honestly. My flatmate calls it a problem. I call it the only bit of my life that makes sense.

own.label: Ask who she lives with
own.player: Do you live with anyone?
own.reply: Jasmin, on the dry river. She calls my giving my wages away a problem. She also eats my soup, so she’s part of the problem.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: Grandad was a founding family’s solicitor, struck off. Dad is a kind drunk who teaches piano. Mum is a Bluebird’s lady’s maid, which I don’t say on campus. Don’t you say it either.

calls.label: Ask about the grant letter
calls.player: Did your group ever get a grant?
calls.reply: A letter signed Ruth Calder says it’s approved, pending a private meeting at the lodge. Just me. On a night I worked out has no moon. I wrote to thank her. She didn’t know anything about it. I haven’t told the group, because they’d say no and the water kit is real.
calls.note: Eden Sutherland has a grant letter signed with Ruth Calder’s name inviting her alone to the lodge on a moonless night; Ruth Calder never sent it.

calls.label: Ask who cries in her choir
calls.player: Does anyone in your choir get upset?
calls.reply: There’s a hymn about the deep that makes a girl from the club cry. Elise. I’m blunt, so I asked her why. She’s started telling me. It’s about an invitation.
calls.note: Eden Sutherland says Elise Harrow has started confiding in her about a frightening invitation.

women.name: Agnes Castillo
women.look: Deep brown skin, box braids to the waist, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, soft cream jumper and long pleated skirt

own.label: Ask about the parish garden
own.player: What grows in a desert parish garden?
own.reply: Roses, if you’re stubborn. Prickly pear, if you’re sensible. We grow both, which is very Catholic of us.

own.label: Ask about the ballroom dancing
own.player: You’re learning ballroom dancing?
own.reply: Yes, and I’m dreadful. It’s good for me. You have to let someone else lead, which I find very hard.

own.label: Ask what she’s worried about
own.player: You seem worried about something.
own.reply: There’s a payment in the parish books to a company I’ve never heard of. Nobody will explain it. I’ve prayed about it and I still want an answer.
own.note: Agnes Castillo found an unexplained parish payment to an unknown company.

own.label: Ask what grows best in the desert
own.player: What grows best in the desert?
own.reply: Things that wait. Seeds sit for years until the rain comes. My grandmother called it faith with roots.

own.label: Ask what else happens in the garden
own.player: What goes on in the chapel garden?
own.reply: Roses, vegetables for the pantry, and a kiln where Alma fires her pots one evening a week. On firing nights the whole garden smells like bread and stones.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What did your father do?
own.reply: He was the Old Mission’s last sacristan. He died there, of a stroke, in the crypt, while he was locking it. My mother still sings in the choir. She won’t go up the mission road.

own.label: Ask if she has a sister
own.player: Do you have any sisters?
own.reply: Freya. Two doors from the Old Mission, with a house full of cacti. We haven’t spoken in six years, over God. I pray for her every night. She’d hate that.

own.label: Ask what her father said at the end
own.player: What did your father say, at the end?
own.reply: He rang me from the crypt, before the stroke took him. He said the bell was ringing, and that it couldn’t ring. That bell has been cracked since before my grandmother was born. I’ve told nobody but God, and now you.
own.note: Agnes Castillo’s father rang her from the Old Mission’s crypt before he died, saying the cracked bell was ringing.

own.label: Ask about the payment in her accounts
own.player: Why is a strange payment in your garden accounts?
own.reply: Because nobody reads the garden accounts. Somebody chose my line on purpose to hide a payment to Halcyon Ridge Consultancy. I’ve prayed about it. God hasn’t told me who. I’m still asking.
own.note: Agnes Castillo says a payment to Halcyon Ridge Consultancy was hidden in her garden accounts.

women.name: Eliza Montoya
women.look: Warm brown skin, box braids to the waist, freckles across her nose, soft cream jumper and long pleated skirt

own.label: Ask about the food pantry
own.player: What’s the food pantry like?
own.reply: Busy and quiet at the same time. People come in ashamed and leave a little less ashamed. That’s the real work. The tins are just the excuse.

own.label: Ask why she volunteers
own.player: Why do you give so much of your time?
own.reply: Because it was given to me first. When my family had nothing, the Sisters fed us and never once made us feel small. I owe them the rest of my life, gladly.

own.label: Ask what’s troubling her
own.player: You seem troubled.
own.reply: The pantry’s storeroom has a filing cabinet nobody uses, and now it’s locked and the key is gone. Someone is keeping something in a place nobody thinks to look.
own.note: Eliza Montoya says an unused filing cabinet in the food pantry’s storeroom is now locked and its key is missing.

own.label: Ask who comes to the pantry
own.player: Who comes to the food pantry?
own.reply: People you’d never guess. A nurse. A man in a suit who cried. Pride is the hardest thing anyone carries through that door.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: Three little brothers, a mum who cleans, and a dad who drove the casino’s deliveries until they let him go without a reason. We had nothing once. We have a little now. The Sisters’ name is said in our house like a saint’s.

own.label: Ask about the cakes she serves
own.player: What do you serve at the pantry?
own.reply: Whatever comes in. A girl from the club brings cakes that always collapse, so I serve them in bowls and call it trifle. Nobody has ever complained.

own.label: Ask about the locked cabinet
own.player: What do you think is in the locked cabinet?
own.reply: Something Margaret is afraid of the bishop finding. Her hand goes to that cabinet when he’s mentioned, and Evelyn’s hand goes to her collar. I’ve worked out they’re the same thing. I haven’t said so. I’m saying it to you because you won’t tell.
own.note: Eliza Montoya believes the pantry’s locked cabinet holds what Margaret Holloway is hiding from the bishop, and Evelyn Rosales wears its key.

women.name: Rosalie Kemp
women.look: Pale skin, sandy shag with a fringe, a beauty mark above her lip, long-sleeved maxi dress

own.label: Ask about the chapel archive
own.player: What’s in the chapel archive?
own.reply: Baptisms, marriages and funerals back to when Sunfall was a mission. Every name in this town is in my books somewhere.

own.label: Ask about her book club
own.player: You run a book club?
own.reply: Six women, one bottle of sherry and a lot of arguing about Jane Austen. It’s the most honest room in the parish.

own.label: Ask what’s troubling her
own.player: Something’s troubling you.
own.reply: Our caretaker vanished without collecting his wages. A man who never missed Mass. He looked after the bell tower.
own.note: Rosalie Kemp says the chapel caretaker, who looked after the bell tower, vanished without collecting his wages.

own.label: Ask what the old records say about love
own.player: What do the old parish records say about love?
own.reply: Marriages that lasted sixty years, recorded in two lines. No photographs, no speeches. Just two names and a lifetime.

own.label: Ask about the registers
own.player: Where do you keep the old registers?
own.reply: In a fireproof room I made the parish build. Every name in Sunfall is in there, two lines per life. If the chapel burns, the town forgets who it is. Not on my watch.

own.label: Ask about her parents
own.player: Are your parents archivists too?
own.reply: Dad kept the school’s records, Mum kept the house’s. They’re retired and spend their days cross-checking each other. It’s very romantic, in a filing sort of way.

own.label: Ask why the Old Mission was closed
own.player: Why did the parish stop using the Old Mission?
own.reply: The register for the thirtieth year: the Beaumont, Blackwood and Van Doren marriages all move to St Brigid’s, and the priest has written that the Old Mission is closed for a reason he will not write down. A priest refusing to write something down. That’s the loudest line in the book.
own.note: Rosalie Kemp’s register shows the founding families stopped marrying at the Old Mission in the thirtieth year, for a reason the priest would not record.

own.label: Ask about the caretaker
own.player: What happened to your caretaker?
own.reply: Aurelio Baca. He kept the bell tower and the Old Mission’s keys. He never missed Mass and he never collected his last wages. Eleven weeks now. Nobody has reported him missing but me.
own.note: Rosalie Kemp says the caretaker Aurelio Baca, who kept the Old Mission’s keys, vanished eleven weeks ago without collecting his wages.

women.name: Bernadette Flores
women.look: Rosy fair skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, sage cardigan and long linen skirt

own.label: Ask about conserving old things
own.player: What does a conservator actually do?
own.reply: I keep beautiful things from falling apart a little longer. Paintings, vestments, people, occasionally.

own.label: Ask why new things look so cheap
own.player: Why does everything new look so cheap?
own.reply: Because we stopped making things to last. Our grandparents built for their grandchildren. We build for the next quarterly report.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: I promised my father I’d marry in the chapel where he married my mother. I nearly gave up on that promise. I’ve started believing in it again.

own.label: Ask why she repairs instead of replaces
own.player: Why repair things instead of replacing them?
own.reply: Because a mended thing has a story. A new thing just has a price. We throw away so much now, people included.

own.label: Ask about her walk to work
own.player: What’s your walk to work like?
own.reply: Past the jeweller’s on Fifth Avenue, where I don’t look in the window, because the owner has twice offered to buy the parish’s old chalice. It isn’t for sale. Nothing that old should be.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What did your father do?
own.reply: He was a carpenter. He built the museum’s display cases, so I work inside his hands every day. He married Mum at St Brigid’s. On his last night he asked me to marry where he had.

own.label: Ask about the Foundation’s loan
own.player: What did the Foundation lend the museum?
own.reply: A brooch, a bell clapper, nine goblets and a book. The inventory calls the book a hymnal and marks it with a crescent. I opened it. It is not a hymnal. I closed it and said a decade of the rosary.
own.note: Bernadette Flores says the Foundation’s loan to the museum includes a bell clapper and a crescent-marked book that is not a hymnal.

women.name: Lucia Romano
women.look: Deep brown skin, long locs with gold cuffs, strong dark brows, blouse with a Peter Pan collar

women.name: Odette Price
women.look: Olive skin, black space buns, amber eyes, rolled-sleeve oxford shirt

own.label: Ask about local radio
own.player: What’s it like working in local radio?
own.reply: Lovely and doomed. The phone-in callers are the loneliest people in town, and they’re the best part of the show.

own.label: Ask about her sketches
own.player: You sketch old shopfronts?
own.reply: Before they’re turned into vape shops. I’ve drawn eleven that are gone now. It’s a sort of memorial.

own.label: Ask about the letter
own.player: Is something worrying you?
own.reply: An unsigned letter came to my flat. It said stop asking about the junction. I hadn’t asked about the junction yet.
own.note: Odette Price got an unsigned letter telling her to stop asking about the junction.

own.label: Ask whose voice she misses
own.player: Is there a voice you miss?
own.reply: My grandfather read the shipping forecast on local radio for thirty years. Nobody needed it in the desert. He read it anyway, like a prayer.

own.label: Ask about her sisters
own.player: Are you one of the Price sisters?
own.reply: One of three. Samantha sells houses, Bethany keeps the library, I keep the radio, which was Grandad’s. We meet once a week at the library to argue. It’s the best hour of my week.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Did your dad work at the station too?
own.reply: He sold the station’s advertising and drank it. Grandad read the shipping forecast in the desert for thirty years. I got the voice from one and the thirst for facts from neither.

calls.label: Ask what she found in the tape archive
calls.player: Found anything in the station’s old tapes?
calls.reply: A reel from forty years ago: a live broadcast from the Old Mission’s fair. Under the noise there’s a bell, which can’t be, and nine voices singing a round. Then the broadcast just stops.
calls.note: Odette Price found a forty-year-old broadcast from the Old Mission with a bell and nine voices singing, which cuts off.

calls.label: Ask what she’s found about the junction
calls.player: What have you found about the junction?
calls.reply: I hadn’t asked about it until the letter told me to stop. Now I have. The weigh station there isn’t abandoned. It’s leased. Someone keeps a light on.
calls.note: Odette Price says the weigh station at the old junction is leased, and someone keeps a light on there.

women.name: Arielle Brooks
women.look: Golden-tan skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, freckles across her nose, bomber jacket and graphic tee

own.label: Ask about the newspaper archive
own.player: What do you find in the Sunfall Daily archive?
own.reply: A hundred years of the town lying to itself in very nice fonts. My favourite headline is from the drought years: Rain Expected Any Day Now. It wasn’t.

own.label: Ask about stargazing
own.player: You go stargazing in the desert?
own.reply: Every clear night. Out past the canyon the sky is so full it’s almost loud. You remember how small Sunfall is, and how small its scandals are.

own.label: Ask about the favour
own.player: Has someone asked you for a favour?
own.reply: An old friend wants me to lose a box of clippings about the old chapel’s last caretaker. She’s never asked me for anything before. That’s what worries me.
own.note: Arielle Brooks was asked by an old friend to lose archive clippings about the old chapel’s last caretaker.

own.label: Ask which star she’d name after you
own.player: If you named a star after me, which one?
own.reply: A dim one. Don’t be offended. The dim ones are the ones you only find if you’re really looking.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: Above the Lucky Cactus. My aunt Dolores raised me and my cousin Zara at that counter after my mum left. Dolores died in the kitchen, and now my cousins run it in shifts and fight about the booth.

own.label: Ask what the archive is like
own.player: What’s it like down in the archive?
own.reply: A hundred years of the town lying to itself in very nice fonts. I know the paper better than anyone alive, which is a lonely thing to know.

calls.label: Ask about the caretaker clippings
calls.player: What’s in the box you’re meant to lose?
calls.reply: Forty years ago the Old Mission’s caretaker, a man called Baca, vanished after a night with no moon and never collected his wages. The paper ran three stories and then nothing. The third names the women seen at the chapel that week. One of them was Honoria Blackwood’s mother. I haven’t lost the box.
calls.note: Arielle Brooks says the Old Mission’s caretaker vanished forty years ago, and Honoria Blackwood’s mother was seen at the chapel that week.

women.name: Harper Lin
women.look: Freckled fair skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, deep dimples, striped shirt and trench coat

own.label: Ask what goes into the weekend paper
own.player: What goes into the weekend paper?
own.reply: Recipes, the crossword and one serious story I fight for every single week. People only read the crossword, so I put the serious story next to it.

own.label: Ask about her old dog
own.player: Tell me about your dog.
own.reply: Pickle. Thirteen, deaf as a post, and asleep under my desk at the paper. She’s our longest-serving member of staff.

own.label: Ask about her favourite headline
own.player: What’s your favourite headline you ever wrote?
own.reply: GOAT EATS MAYOR’S SPEECH. True story. It was a very good speech, apparently. The goat agreed.

own.label: Ask about a story she never ran
own.player: Is there a story you never ran?
own.reply: One. The facts were right and it would have ruined a good woman for one bad week. I spiked it. I still don’t know if that was journalism or cowardice.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Were your parents writers too?
own.reply: Teachers. Dad taught at the parish school before Teresa Bellamy, Mum at the hill school. I was a bright, kind girl who became a bright, kind reporter, and found out that isn’t enough at the city desk.

own.label: Ask what she collects
own.player: Do you collect anything?
own.reply: Dogs and reporters. Strays, mostly. Pickle was the first and is still in charge.

calls.label: Ask who the story she spiked was about
calls.player: Who was the story you spiked about?
calls.reply: My ex-fiancé’s new wife, the week before their wedding. She’d been up at the lodge the week a man died there. Her name was Veronica Shawcross. He was voted into the family that spring and buried that winter. I still don’t know if I was being kind or a coward.
calls.note: Harper Lin says her ex-fiancé married Veronica Shawcross, was voted in, and died within the year.

women.name: Delia Maher
women.look: Pale skin, twist-out coils, deep dimples, rolled-sleeve oxford shirt

own.label: Ask how she got so far so young
own.player: You’re young for an investigative reporter.
own.reply: I’m patient for a young person. That’s the trick. Everyone else my age wants to go viral. I want to be right.

own.label: Ask about her old cameras
own.player: You restore old film cameras?
own.reply: Film makes you think before you shoot. Digital lets you shoot instead of thinking. Same with opinions.

own.label: Ask about the ruined recording
own.player: What’s on the recording you’re restoring?
own.reply: A voicemail from the night of the gala. Half of it is static. The other half is a woman saying not Table 9, the kitchen.
own.note: Delia Maher is restoring a gala-night voicemail: a woman says not Table 9, the kitchen.

own.label: Ask if she ever feels too young for her job
own.player: Do you ever feel too young for your job?
own.reply: Every press conference. Old men call me sweetheart, and then they read what I wrote about them. Nobody calls me sweetheart twice.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What does your dad do?
own.reply: He was a signalman. He taught me to listen to the line for the train before you could see it. That’s all reporting is, really.

own.label: Ask where her patience comes from
own.player: Where does the patience come from?
own.reply: My mum died of something slow when I was ten. You learn patience sitting by a bed. You learn that the end comes on its own schedule, not yours.

own.label: Ask about her camera from an estate sale
own.player: Where did you get your camera?
own.reply: Daria sold it to me from an estate sale. There was a roll still inside, never developed. The estate belonged to a Bluebird husband. I haven’t developed it yet. I’m being patient again.

calls.label: Ask what the cleaned recording says
calls.player: What’s on the cleaned-up voicemail?
calls.reply: Alisha helped me clean it. After the woman says not Table 9, the kitchen, there’s a man’s voice saying a name: Marchbanks. Then a door. I won’t print until I know the woman’s name. Right beats first.
calls.note: Delia Maher’s cleaned voicemail from gala night has a man saying the name Marchbanks.

women.name: Zadie Foster
women.look: Light-brown skin, ash-blonde lob, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, utility vest with many pockets

own.label: Ask about reviewing music
own.player: What’s reviewing music like?
own.reply: Free tickets and a lot of enemies. Bands remember a bad review forever. One drummer still sends me a postcard every year that just says no.

own.label: Ask if she’s any good at pool
own.player: Are you any good at pool?
own.reply: Dangerously. My neighbours play for washing-up duty. I haven’t washed a plate in two years.

own.label: Ask about the best gig she’s seen
own.player: What’s the best gig you’ve ever seen?
own.reply: A girl with a broken guitar in the back room of the Lucky Cactus. Eleven people. She played like there were thousands. I gave her five stars and she cried.

own.label: Ask if she’d ever stop writing
own.player: Would you ever stop writing?
own.reply: Every rejection makes me want to. Then I hear a song I need to tell someone about, and I’m back. It’s less a job than an affliction.

own.label: Ask about her neighbour
own.player: Do you get on with your neighbours?
own.reply: Sienna next door teaches herself the drums very badly. I bang on the wall in time. It’s become a band. We have a name. We will never perform.

own.label: Ask if she ever played music
own.player: Did you ever play?
own.reply: Cello, in the Blue Ribbon Youth Orchestra, at twelve. Beside Hannah Webb and a girl who calls herself Salem now. I was bad at it, which is why I became a critic.

calls.label: Ask about the old orchestra programmes
calls.player: What did you find in the old programmes?
calls.reply: I kept the youth orchestra’s programmes from the year before and the year after. The first says sponsored by Ellis Dane. The second says the Blue Ribbon Foundation. Same orchestra, same kids, different name. I never thought about it until Hannah asked.
calls.note: Zadie Foster’s old programmes show the youth orchestra’s sponsor changed from Ellis Dane to the Blue Ribbon Foundation.

women.name: Celina Rojas
women.look: Warm beige skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, rosy cheeks, press lanyard and denim jacket

own.label: Ask what a photography assistant does
own.player: What does a photography assistant actually do?
own.reply: Carry everything, hold the reflector and get blamed for the weather. One day I’ll take the picture. Today I hold the bag.

own.label: Ask about the bicycle
own.player: How’s the bike coming along?
own.reply: It has two wheels now. Neither of them goes round. I’ve watched forty videos about chains and I understand less than when I started.

own.label: Ask about the best picture she’s helped take
own.player: What’s the best picture you’ve helped take?
own.reply: An old cowboy at the rodeo, laughing with no teeth. My boss got the credit. I got the cowboy’s number. He rings me on my birthday.

own.label: Ask what keeps her up at night
own.player: What keeps you up at night?
own.reply: Whether I’m good enough or just keen. Whether keen runs out. Whether you can tell I reread my messages six times before I send them.

own.label: Ask where she used to live
own.player: Have you always lived above your mum’s café?
own.reply: No. In the spring I had a room above the laundromat on Sunfall Road. The radiator sang at night. I left in one night and I don’t talk about why. If you’re in that room now, the third floorboard from the door creaks. Sorry.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What are your family like?
own.reply: Mum runs a café the Daily’s night staff live in. Dad rode the rodeo with Diana Moore’s first husband, until a fall. He’s in a chair now and still the funniest man in the county.

own.label: Ask about the cowboy who rings her
own.player: Who rings you on your birthday?
own.reply: An old cowboy from Dad’s rodeo days. Every year, same joke, same song, badly. I’d be devastated if he stopped.

own.label: Ask if she knows Moira Bell
own.player: Do you know Moira Bell?
own.reply: My friend. My best one, maybe. If she’s ringing you a lot, that’s a bad patch, and her mum’s the one who can help. Ruth Bell. Here: {number}. Tell her Celina sent you.
own.note: Celina Rojas, Moira’s friend, gave you the number for Moira’s mother, Ruth Bell.

calls.label: Ask why she left the room above the laundromat
calls.player: Why did you leave the laundromat room in one night?
calls.reply: A letter under the door, unsigned, in handwriting I’ve since seen on the Foundation’s Christmas cards. It said my photograph of Valerie Huxley for the society page showed a woman who was unwell, that I wouldn’t take another, and that the room wasn’t safe for a girl who looked at Bluebirds through a lens. I packed while the radiator sang.
calls.note: Celina Rojas, the last tenant of the room above the laundromat, left after an unsigned letter in a Foundation hand warned her off photographing Bluebirds.

women.name: Kira Henson
women.look: Warm beige skin, burgundy-dyed curls, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, cable-knit jumper and leather satchel

own.label: Ask what court reporting is like
own.player: What’s court reporting like?
own.reply: I sit in the same room as the worst things people do and write down every word. You learn to hear what people don’t say. The pauses are where the truth is.

own.label: Ask where her hidden routes go
own.player: Where do your hidden hiking routes go?
own.reply: Old mining paths, dry riverbeds, a cave nobody marks on the map. I draw them by hand, and I only share them with people I trust.

own.label: Ask about her oldest friend
own.player: Who’s your oldest friend?
own.reply: A girl from my first newsroom. We fell out for six years over nothing. Then her dad died and I was on her doorstep within the hour. That’s friendship. Turning up.

own.label: Ask if a verdict ever felt wrong
own.player: Has a verdict ever felt wrong to you?
own.reply: Once. I wrote it up straight, the way you have to. Then I walked into the desert and stayed until dark. The desert doesn’t argue.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A cabin on the canyon side with a wall of maps I drew by hand. Old mining paths, dry riverbeds. And one cave I have never marked and never will.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Who taught you shorthand?
own.reply: My father kept the county court’s records for forty years and taught me shorthand at eight. He died two years ago. My oldest friend was on the doorstep within the hour. That’s what friendship is: turning up.

calls.label: Ask about the pause in the inquest
calls.player: What did the pauses tell you in court?
calls.reply: The Sanderson inquest. The coroner asked the Foundation’s driver where he’d been that night. Nine seconds of nothing. Then an answer that was struck from the record. It’s still in my shorthand: the lodge.
calls.note: Kira Henson’s shorthand of the Sanderson inquest records that the Foundation’s driver said he had been at the lodge, an answer struck from the record.

women.name: Moira Bell
women.look: Waifish and very pale, a slim small-busted model figure, faint shadows under dark sullen eyes, bleached eyebrows, golden-brown ringlets, a small nose stud, a striped shirt under an oversized trench coat

own.label: Ask what a fact-checker does
own.player: What does a fact-checker actually do?
own.reply: I ring people and ask if they really said what they said. Most of them didn’t. I remember everything anyone tells me. It’s a gift, mostly.

own.label: Ask about teaching her cousin guitar
own.player: How are the guitar lessons going?
own.reply: He’s eleven and only wants to learn one song. I’ve taught it to him eighty times. I don’t mind. I like it when people need me.

own.label: Ask why she hates small talk
own.player: Why do you hate small talk?
own.reply: Because it’s a waste of a person. I’d rather know one true thing about you than a hundred nice ones. Tell me one true thing.

own.label: Ask what she remembers about you
own.player: What do you remember about me so far?
own.reply: Everything. What you said first, what you didn’t answer, how long you took to reply. Sorry. That came out intense. It’s the job.

own.label: Ask about her cousin
own.player: Who’s the cousin you teach?
own.reply: Ollie. Eleven. He only wants to learn one song and I’ve taught it to him eighty times. I don’t mind. I like being needed. That’s probably the problem.

own.label: Ask about her mum
own.player: What’s your mum like?
own.reply: Ruth. She cleans at the hospital and comes home with her feet in a bowl. She’s the strongest person I know and the most tired.

calls.label: Ask about the letters to the editor
calls.player: What’s in the box of letters you keep?
calls.reply: Forty letters to the editor from one man, every one in verse, every one with the same return address: the flat above the old Rialto. I keep the envelopes. I remember everything, so I remember where he lives.
calls.note: Moira Bell keeps Theon’s forty letters to the editor; they all come from the flat above the old Rialto.

calls.label: Ask about her dad
calls.player: What happened to your dad?
calls.reply: He was a signalman. He died on the line when I was nine. I saved a voicemail from the week before: he’d be late because the Foundation’s lorry was on the crossing again and he had to log it. I rang the Foundation. They said there was no lorry. I remember everything.
calls.note: Moira Bell’s late father logged a Foundation lorry on the railway crossing the week before he died; the Foundation denies it.

women.name: Talia Farouk
women.look: Light olive skin, layered caramel shoulder-length hair, tortoiseshell glasses, rolled-sleeve oxford shirt

own.label: Ask about her travel column
own.player: What do you write about in your travel column?
own.reply: Places nobody visits on purpose. A motel with one working sign, a diner with the best pie for two hundred miles. Readers send me hate mail and then go there.

own.label: Ask about her forgotten records
own.player: What kind of records do you collect?
own.reply: Ones nobody else remembers. Singers who made one album and vanished. I like to think somebody somewhere is still singing in the shower, unaware they’re a cult classic.

own.label: Ask what she’s sceptical of
own.player: What are you sceptical of?
own.reply: Hidden gems. Every hidden gem has a gift shop now. The real ones don’t know they’re hidden.

own.label: Ask where she feels at home
own.player: Where do you feel most at home?
own.reply: On a bus at night, with nowhere to be for six hours. Everyone else calls it travel. I call it the only time my head is quiet.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Does travel run in your family?
own.reply: Grandad drove the first bus route from Sunfall to the coast. Dad runs what’s left of it: two coaches and a timetable. I grew up asleep across the back seats.

own.label: Ask where the best pie is
own.player: Where’s the best pie in the county?
own.reply: A diner two hundred miles from here with a waitress who calls everyone sugar. I won’t print the name. Some things should only be found.

calls.label: Ask about her letter
calls.player: What did your unsigned letter say?
calls.reply: That the weigh station at the old junction is private property. It isn’t. I checked. It belongs to the county and it’s leased to a trust. Someone wanted me to think it was none of my business, which is how I knew it was.
calls.note: Talia Farouk found that the weigh station at the old junction belongs to the county and is leased to a trust.
