women.name: Sable Marlow
women.look: Light olive skin, dark French braid, a beauty mark above her lip, black lace corset top

own.label: Ask about running a music venue
own.player: What’s it like running a venue?
own.reply: Glamorous for ten minutes a night. The rest is mopping and arguing with drummers.

own.label: Ask about her football
own.player: You play five-a-side?
own.reply: Goalkeeper. I like standing in the way of things. Ask my exes.

own.label: Ask about the borrowed camera
own.player: Why did you borrow someone’s camera?
own.reply: The house photographer left it behind after the last goth night. One photo’s been deleted. Who deletes one photo? Someone with something in it.
own.note: A camera left at Sable Marlow’s venue after goth night has one deleted photo.

own.label: Ask about the best night at her venue
own.player: What was the best night your venue ever had?
own.reply: A band nobody had heard of played to forty people in a storm. The power cut, and they kept going acoustic. Nobody went home.

own.label: Ask how she got the venue
own.player: How did you get the Cellar Door?
own.reply: It was my dad’s bar. A chain bought it off him and I bought it back off the chain, with a loan from the casino’s bank I’ll be paying till I die. Mum sings in a chapel on the state road. She prays for my overdraft.

own.label: Ask about the goalkeeper gloves on her hook
own.player: Do you still play in goal?
own.reply: Every week. Women’s five-a-side. I like standing in the way of things. My exes all say that as if it’s an insult.

calls.label: Ask what was in the deleted photo
calls.player: Did you ever get the deleted photo back?
calls.reply: I restored it off the card. It’s the photographer’s little sister, Sorrel, handing an envelope to a man at the back of my room. Dorian Kell. He sits at the back of my goth nights in a charity lanyard. I haven’t said so, because the casino’s bank holds my loan.
calls.note: Sable Marlow restored a photo of Sorrel Vane handing an envelope to Dorian Kell at the Cellar Door.

women.name: Lenore Vale
women.look: Golden-tan skin, sandy shag with a fringe, strong dark brows, studded leather jacket

own.label: Ask if she’s related to Professor Vale
own.player: Any relation to Professor Vale?
own.reply: None. Probably. My grandmother would have said every Vale is cousin to a scandal.

own.label: Ask about her jewellery
own.player: What do you make?
own.reply: Silver mourning jewellery. Lockets for hair, rings for the dead. People think it’s morbid. I think it’s love that refuses to stop.

own.label: Ask about her strangest order
own.player: What’s the strangest order you’ve had?
own.reply: Thirteen crescent pendants, paid in cash, collected by a girl who wouldn’t take her sunglasses off. I make a mark on everything I cast. I’d know them anywhere.
own.note: Lenore Vale cast thirteen crescent pendants for a cash order, and marks everything she makes.

own.label: Ask what she’d make for someone she loved
own.player: What would you make for someone you loved?
own.reply: A ring that doesn’t look like a ring. Something only the two of us would know meant anything.

own.label: Ask who taught her
own.player: Who taught you to make jewellery?
own.reply: Josephine Mercer, at the Canal Bench. I’m her best apprentice and she’ll never say so. She tells me my solder is lazy. It isn’t. It’s confident.

own.label: Ask what she does after work
own.player: What do you do when the bench closes?
own.reply: I play drums in a lock-up. There’s another woman in the next lock-up who plays even worse. We’ve never spoken. It’s the best relationship I’ve had.

calls.label: Ask who’s wearing her pendants
calls.player: Have you seen your crescents on anyone?
calls.reply: I’d know my mark across a room. A reporter bought a thirtieth. Hex and Ivy wear theirs. A man in a charity lanyard had one at the Vestry. And there’s one painted on the bottom of a cup somebody brought me.
calls.note: Lenore Vale has seen her crescent pendants on Hex Morrow, Ivy Sable and a man in a charity lanyard.

calls.label: Ask about the ring nobody collected
calls.player: Is there anything at the bench nobody collected?
calls.reply: My uncle’s ring. The Bluebirds gave it to him, a husband’s signet, as a favour. I resized it. He never came for it. There’s a crescent inside the band.
calls.note: Lenore Vale has Professor Vale’s uncollected signet ring from the Bluebirds, with a crescent inside.

women.name: Ashlyn Vex
women.look: Dark skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, a small nose stud, velvet choker and black slip dress

own.label: Ask about running the venue
own.player: What’s it like running a music venue?
own.reply: Mopping beer off the floor at the end of the night while a band argues about their fee. I wouldn’t swap it for anything. The floor is sticky with history.

own.label: Ask why she’s learning Italian
own.player: Why are you learning Italian?
own.reply: So I can be dramatic in a language that deserves it. English doesn’t have enough words for despair. Italian has a whole opera.

own.label: Ask about the worst band she’s booked
own.player: Who’s the worst band you’ve ever booked?
own.reply: A trio who played one note, very slowly, for an hour. They called it a protest. Against what, nobody found out. They sold out.

own.label: Ask what she’s restless for
own.player: What are you restless for?
own.reply: Somewhere that isn’t here. Then I get there and miss the sticky floor. I think home is just the place you complain about most.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: My mum ran a boarding house in Old Town. I grew up among lodgers. One was a young drama tutor called Leonard Kitteridge, who taught me to project. It’s flats now.

own.label: Ask how she started
own.player: How did you end up running the Rialto?
own.reply: I came in at nineteen as a barmaid and never left. Nine years managing the ballroom now. The floor’s sticky with history and I know every board that creaks.

calls.label: Ask who lives above the ballroom
calls.player: Who lives in the flat above your ballroom?
calls.reply: Theon. The one who reads in verse through my ceiling every night. He climbs those stairs at all hours. The flat above the old Rialto, if you need it on a map.
calls.note: Ashlyn Vex says Theon lives in the flat above the old Rialto’s ballroom.

calls.label: Ask why she lets him stay
calls.player: Why do you let him stay up there?
calls.reply: The landlord’s company asked me to, in a letter, with a rent cut. A company with a made-up name. I’ve worked out why since: the Rialto is the next shopfront to go, and a tenant like him is a reason to close it.
calls.note: Ashlyn Vex says a company with a made-up name pays to keep Theon in the Rialto flat, to have an excuse to close the building.

women.name: Morrigan Hale
women.look: Fair skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, tortoiseshell glasses, black lace corset top

own.label: Ask about her jewellery
own.player: What kind of jewellery do you make?
own.reply: Silver bats, tiny coffins, rings shaped like thorns. Brides buy them for their bridesmaids now. Goth has gone mainstream, and I’ve never been richer or sadder.

own.label: Ask about her collages
own.player: What do you make collages from?
own.reply: Old funeral cards and pressed flowers. It sounds morbid. It’s the most hopeful thing I do. Everyone in them was loved by someone.

own.label: Ask if she really breaks hearts
own.player: Is it true you break hearts?
own.reply: I don’t break them. I just leave before they get attached, and that hurts more than breaking. I’m working on staying. Slowly.

own.label: Ask what would make her stay
own.player: What would make you stay?
own.reply: Someone who notices when I go quiet and doesn’t panic. Someone who makes tea and waits. That’s all. Nobody waits.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are you related to the Hales at the Daily?
own.reply: Beatrice and Brittany are my cousins. Dad sells sports goods and never understood a daughter who wore black at twelve. I renamed myself. He still calls me Mo.

own.label: Ask about the empty chair in her flat
own.player: Who’s the spare chair for?
own.reply: Someone who notices when I go quiet and doesn’t panic. I keep it free. Optimism, in furniture form.

calls.label: Ask why her orders stopped
calls.player: Why have your bridal orders stopped?
calls.reply: I said no to Victoria in the Black Lace shop, in front of Piper. She smiled. Since then my brides have cancelled one by one, and every cancellation comes with a crescent drawn on the envelope.
calls.note: Morrigan Hale refused Victoria Blackwood’s invitation, and since then her customers cancel with a crescent drawn on the envelope.

women.name: Cleo Rook
women.look: Pale skin, box braids to the waist, sharp winged eyeliner, long black velvet coat

own.label: Ask about her venue
own.player: What’s your venue like?
own.reply: An old converted church with bad acoustics and a good bar. I’ve run it for twelve years. The bands get younger. The ghosts stay the same.

own.label: Ask about her travel journal
own.player: Where has your travel journal been?
own.reply: Lisbon, Prague, a bus station in the middle of nowhere for nine hours. I write by hand, because a phone forgets and paper doesn’t.

own.label: Ask what she’s proudest of
own.player: What are you proudest of?
own.reply: Never selling the venue to the people who wanted to turn it into flats. They offered a lot. I told them it was haunted. It is.

own.label: Ask about the ghost
own.player: Is your venue really haunted?
own.reply: Something hums in the old vestry when the room is empty. I leave the light on for it. Everyone deserves someone who leaves a light on.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Do you live at the Vestry?
own.reply: In the old presbytery next door. The priest’s rooms. I sleep where a man used to write sermons. I write set lists. Same energy.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Have you got family?
own.reply: My mum was a nurse. She died when I was twenty. My father is unknown, including to my mother, she said, laughing. I came here from nowhere in particular and stayed.

calls.label: Ask what the hum really is
calls.player: What’s actually humming in the old vestry?
calls.reply: A bell. When the church was deconsecrated they meant to send it to the Old Mission to replace its cracked one. It never went. It’s in my cellar under the bar. On nights with no moon it hums, as if something somewhere is ringing a note it answers.
calls.note: Cleo Rook says the Vestry’s old bell, meant for the Old Mission, is in her cellar and hums on moonless nights.

calls.label: Ask if anyone wants the bell
calls.player: Has anyone asked about the bell?
calls.reply: A woman from the club, Delphine, asked to borrow it for the founders’ anniversary. I said I’d think about it. I’ve thought about it. The answer is getting louder.
calls.note: Cleo Rook says Delphine Moreau asked to borrow the Vestry’s bell for the Bluebirds’ founders’ anniversary.

women.name: Veda Thorn
women.look: Dark skin, honey-blonde beach waves, freckles across her nose, long black velvet coat

own.label: Ask how she makes her jewellery
own.player: How do you make your pieces?
own.reply: Lost-wax casting, a gas torch and swearing. The swearing is what gives them character.

own.label: Ask about her film night
own.player: What do you show at your film night?
own.reply: Old horror films in a back room with a bedsheet for a screen. The jumps are better when the projector jumps too.

own.label: Ask why she skips small talk
own.player: Why do you skip the small talk?
own.reply: Because I’d rather argue with you about whether vampires are romantic. They’re not. They’re landlords.

own.label: Ask how she stays calm in a crisis
own.player: How do you stay so calm in a crisis?
own.reply: I fall apart beforehand, in private, in great detail. When the crisis comes I’m all used up. Calm is just exhaustion with good posture.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Is your family arty too?
own.reply: Nurses. Mum’s a ward sister, Gran was the hospital’s first matron. They fix bodies. I cast silver and swear. We’re all in the business of things that last.

own.label: Ask about her torch
own.player: Is that torch dangerous?
own.reply: It was Juno’s. She gave it to me when her hands got tired. I’ve set fire to one eyebrow and two opinions. Both grew back.

calls.label: Ask what the deleted film-night photo showed
calls.player: What was in the frame someone deleted?
calls.reply: My film night’s front row. Hex Morrow, next to a man in a charity lanyard and a boy holding a library book. Hex borrowed my camera to check the shot and deleted it. I restore things. I restored it.
calls.note: Veda Thorn restored a film-night photo of Hex Morrow beside a man in a charity lanyard and a boy with a library book.

women.name: Nixie Adler
women.look: Freckled fair skin, dark French braid, thin wire-rimmed glasses, plum corset dress

own.label: Ask about her roadside souvenirs
own.player: What’s in your souvenir collection?
own.reply: A snow globe of a petrol station, a plastic alien from a diner and a spoon from a town with a population of nine. I love things nobody else would keep.

own.label: Ask what running the venue taught her
own.player: What has running the venue taught you?
own.reply: That the quiet kid at the back will be famous in five years, and the loud one will owe me money. Every time.

own.label: Ask what she’s sceptical of
own.player: What are you sceptical of?
own.reply: Anyone who says they’re an old soul. Babe, you’re twenty-two. I have socks older than your soul.

own.label: Ask who looked after her when she was young
own.player: Who looked after you when you were young?
own.reply: A woman who ran a record shop and let me sit there all day when home was bad. I run the venue for kids like me. Somebody has to leave the door open.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: The motel strip, in a bad house. At eleven I found a record shop in the Old Quarter where a woman let me sit all day and never asked why. She left me enough for the Furnace’s first year.

own.label: Ask why she runs the venue
own.player: Why run a venue?
own.reply: For kids like me. Somebody has to leave the door open. Mind you, sometimes the wrong people walk in through it.

calls.label: Ask who the record shop woman was
calls.player: Who was the woman at the record shop?
calls.reply: Marjorie. Honoria Blackwood’s cousin, disowned for the shop. Before she died she wrote me a letter telling me who Victoria really was, before the scene knew. It says the Blackwood women aren’t to be trusted with the moon.
calls.note: Nixie Adler has a letter from Honoria Blackwood’s cousin saying Victoria is a Blackwood and the Blackwood women aren’t to be trusted with the moon.

calls.label: Ask about the kids who go missing into the scene
calls.player: Who have you seen get pulled in?
calls.reply: Three lost kids this year: Hex, Sorrel, and a boy called Ethan Oakley. I watched the circle find them in my room and I didn’t stop it. I don’t stop kids finding things. I’m starting to think I should have.
calls.note: Nixie Adler watched the circle recruit Hex Morrow, Sorrel Vane and Ethan Oakley at the Furnace.

women.name: Lavinia Gravesend
women.look: Thin and very pale, a long narrow face with hollow cheeks, kohl-smudged dark sullen eyes, a slim small-busted figure, a glossy black ponytail, a black mesh top and a tartan skirt

own.label: Ask about her jewellery
own.player: What do you make?
own.reply: Lockets, mostly. People put photographs and locks of hair in them, the way people did a hundred and fifty years ago. It sounds creepy. It’s the most romantic thing in the world.

own.label: Ask about her watercolours
own.player: What do you paint?
own.reply: The desert in the evening, very badly. I paint everything purple. My tutor said that’s not how colour works. I said that’s how it works for me.

own.label: Ask what she’s noticed about you
own.player: What have you noticed about me?
own.reply: You ask questions and then actually wait for the answer. That’s rarer than you’d think. Most men are just reloading.

own.label: Ask what she’d put in her own locket
own.player: What would you put in your own locket?
own.reply: Nothing yet. I keep it empty on purpose. It feels like a promise I haven’t made to anyone.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: The trailer park behind the drive-in. It produced a goth, a Bluebird, a lab analyst and me. My friend Taryn says that’s a representative sample.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: Halfway up the ridge road, with Brad. The view is amazing. Ask me about the view. Don’t ask me about Brad.

calls.label: Ask about the purple painting
calls.player: What’s the purple painting in your flat?
calls.reply: From my balcony I watched a van with no plates, a crate with air holes, and men with a laptop. And Brad getting in. I painted it all purple. It hangs on our wall and he thinks it’s a sunset.
calls.note: Lavinia Gravesend saw her boyfriend Brad Keller with the van with no plates and a crate with air holes on the ridge road.

women.name: Raven Solis
women.look: Pale skin, platinum pixie cut, strong dark brows, black mesh top and tartan skirt

own.label: Ask what it’s like running a venue so young
own.player: What’s it like running a venue at your age?
own.reply: Bands think I’m the merch girl until I tell them their fee. Then they think I’m terrifying. Both are true.

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: You sing in a choir?
own.reply: I sing hymns in black lipstick. The old ladies were scared of me for a month. Now they knit me scarves. Black ones, specially.

own.label: Ask why she’s so mysterious
own.player: Why are you so mysterious?
own.reply: I’m not. I just don’t know what to say most of the time, so I say nothing, and people decide it means something.

own.label: Ask what she’d sing if nobody was listening
own.player: What would you sing if nobody was listening?
own.reply: Something cheerful. A really stupid pop song. Don’t tell anyone. It would ruin the whole thing I’ve got going.

own.label: Ask who looks after her
own.player: Who looks after you?
own.reply: My aunt Mireya. She’s a police officer and pays for my room above the hall and pretends she doesn’t. I pretend not to know. It works for both of us.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: What was your mum like?
own.reply: Carmen. The beautiful one, everyone says. She died when I was six. The file says overdose. I sing because she did.

calls.label: Ask what the circle wants from her
calls.player: Has anyone asked you to sing somewhere strange?
calls.reply: Victoria wants me as the circle’s voice. I said nothing, and she took that as yes. There’s an invitation with my name on it in the hall’s letterbox. I haven’t opened it.
calls.note: Raven Solis has been invited by Victoria Blackwood to sing at the rite.

calls.label: Ask about the old hymn
calls.player: What’s the old hymn you learned?
calls.reply: Priya found it in the old books and asked the altos to try it. I can sing it. It’s the same round that’s on the circle’s tape. I might be the only person in Sunfall who knows both sides’ music.
calls.note: Raven Solis says the old hymn in St Brigid’s books is the same round the circle uses.

women.name: Ophelia Byrne
women.look: Deep brown skin, chestnut high ponytail, gold hoop earrings, black mesh top and tartan skirt

women.name: Nyx Calder
women.look: Light-brown skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, tortoiseshell glasses, black mesh top and tartan skirt

women.name: Selene Ward
women.look: Pale skin, cornrows into a low bun, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, velvet choker and black slip dress

women.name: Billie Wraith
women.look: Warm brown skin, blunt black bob, sharp winged eyeliner, plum corset dress

women.name: Indigo Crossley
women.look: Rosy fair skin, long red curls, tortoiseshell glasses, plum corset dress

women.name: Moth Delaney
women.look: Warm brown skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, a beauty mark above her lip, silver-buckled platform boots and black jeans

women.name: Ivy Sable
women.look: Warm brown skin, honey-blonde beach waves, a silver ear cuff, black lace corset top

women.name: Astrid Sorrow
women.look: Freckled fair skin, glossy black ponytail, a silver ear cuff, fishnet sleeves under a band tee

women.name: Salem Bell
women.look: Medium-brown skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, a small nose stud, velvet choker and black slip dress

women.name: Coraline Dusk
women.look: Freckled fair skin, jet-black waist-length hair, a gap-toothed smile, velvet choker and black slip dress

women.name: Juno Varela
women.look: Deep brown skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, a gap-toothed smile, long black velvet coat

women.name: Lilith Kestrel
women.look: Dark skin, dark brown messy bun, grey-green eyes, silver-buckled platform boots and black jeans

women.name: Ezraine Quinn
women.look: Warm beige skin, cornrows into a low bun, rosy cheeks, velvet choker and black slip dress

women.name: Eris Moon
women.look: Warm brown skin, platinum pixie cut, thin wire-rimmed glasses, plum corset dress

women.name: Marlowe Poe
women.look: Pale skin, glossy black ponytail, a small nose stud, long black velvet coat

women.name: Wren Black
women.look: Light-brown skin, copper waist-length waves, strong dark brows, studded leather jacket

women.name: Milena Kovac
women.look: Warm brown skin, short silver-dyed crop, a wide bright smile, black mesh top and tartan skirt

women.name: Vesper Lane
women.look: Warm brown skin, long red curls, strong dark brows, plum corset dress

women.name: Hex Morrow
women.look: Olive skin, chestnut high ponytail, amber eyes, long black velvet coat

women.name: Dahlia Grieve
women.look: Deep brown skin, short silver-dyed crop, grey-green eyes, velvet choker and black slip dress

women.name: Sorrel Vane
women.look: Deep brown skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, tortoiseshell glasses, black lace corset top

women.name: Kayla Mendoza
women.look: Dark skin, blunt black bob, grey-green eyes, floral blouse and jeans

own.label: Ask about decorating people’s homes
own.player: What’s it like decorating people’s homes?
own.reply: Everyone wants a calm neutral palette and then cries when they see it. I tell them grey is a mood, not a personality.

own.label: Ask about her film night
own.player: What do you show at your film night?
own.reply: Romcoms, unapologetically. The neighbours bring wine and shout at the screen when he runs to the airport. We know he’ll make it. We need him to.

own.label: Ask about her worst impulse buy
own.player: What’s your worst impulse buy?
own.reply: A velvet sofa the colour of a flamingo. It doesn’t fit through my door. It lives in my sister’s garage. I visit it.

own.label: Ask what her own home is like
own.player: What’s your own home like?
own.reply: Unfinished. I do everyone else’s and never mine. I think I’m waiting until there’s someone to choose the curtains with.

own.label: Ask about her daughter
own.player: Do you have children?
own.reply: Nikki, nineteen. I had her at sixteen and my family were horrified for about a year, then adored her. She works nights at the pharmacy and is sharper than me.

own.label: Ask about her film night
own.player: Who comes to your film nights?
own.reply: The neighbours, with wine. We watch romcoms and shout at the airport scene. We know he makes it. We need him to.

calls.label: Ask about the job she can’t photograph
calls.player: Have you ever done a job you couldn’t show anyone?
calls.reply: The lodge’s dining room, through the jeweller, cash, no photographs. The table seats nine. The ninth chair, at the end, has a blue ribbon on it, and the client asked me to match the fabric to the ribbon.
calls.note: Kayla Mendoza decorated the lodge’s dining room: a table for nine, with a blue ribbon on the ninth chair.

women.name: Brittany Hale
women.look: Light-brown skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, sharp winged eyeliner, turquoise peasant top

own.label: Ask about her souvenirs
own.player: What do you collect?
own.reply: Roadside souvenirs! A snow globe of a cactus, a spoon from a motel that burned down, a fridge magnet of the bear. I need help.

own.label: Ask about being a florist
own.player: What’s the best part of being a florist?
own.reply: Weddings. The worst part is weddings. Brides cry, mothers cry, I cry, the flowers wilt.

own.label: Ask what’s confusing her
own.player: Is something confusing you?
own.reply: Two people told me completely different stories about the same night of the gala. One of them is lying, and they both bought peonies.

own.label: Ask what flowers say that people can’t
own.player: What do flowers say that people can’t?
own.reply: Sorry, mostly. I sell more sorry than love. Men walk in looking at the floor and point at the roses.

own.label: Ask where she finds her souvenirs
own.player: Where do you find your souvenirs?
own.reply: The same market on Sundays. There’s a whole gang of us who buy spoons and snow globes and never once talk about anything but spoons. It’s very restful.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: What’s your sister like?
own.reply: Beatrice runs on a bad knee and good coffee. She told me a man at the club once called me a lovely sister. It wasn’t a compliment. She bought me a door chain.

calls.label: Ask about the two peony buyers
calls.player: Who were the two customers with different stories?
calls.reply: Eloise Rainer said she was at the kitchen door laughing with a man who left through it. Simone Ellery swore nobody left by the kitchen and Eloise wasn’t even there. Both bought peonies for the same table. One of them is lying. I write down what customers tell me, for the cards. Mr Kell came in twice for peonies too.
calls.note: Brittany Hale heard Eloise Rainer and Simone Ellery give opposite accounts of the club’s kitchen door on gala night.

women.name: Nina Petrov
women.look: Rosy fair skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, thin wire-rimmed glasses, sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask about her bakery
own.player: How did a pastry chef end up in the desert?
own.reply: I followed a man here from St Petersburg. The man left. The ovens stayed. I chose the ovens.

own.label: Ask about her painting
own.player: You paint watercolours?
own.reply: Desert landscapes. Watercolour is like this town: you can’t correct a mistake, only paint over it and hope.

own.label: Ask about the torn page
own.player: Why do you keep a torn notebook?
own.reply: A customer left a notebook at the counter with one page torn out. The next page shows the impression of the writing: a list of table numbers and a time I can’t read.
own.note: Nina Petrov has a notebook left at her counter; the page after a torn-out one shows an impression of table numbers.

own.label: Ask what she’d do over
own.player: If you could do one thing over, what would it be?
own.reply: I’d have said yes to a man who asked me to dance at a wedding in my twenties. I said I was tired. I wasn’t tired.

own.label: Ask what the bakery is known for
own.player: What should I order at your bakery?
own.reply: The rye, and the Napoleon. The club orders the Napoleon for its small dinners. The Sisters order rye for the volunteers. I prefer the Sisters.

own.label: Ask when she paints
own.player: When do you paint?
own.reply: At dawn, before the dough. Badly, which is the point. Watercolour is like this town: you can’t fix a mistake, only paint over it and hope.

calls.label: Ask about the notebook in her till
calls.player: What’s in the notebook you keep in the till?
calls.reply: A customer left it a week before the benefit. A page was torn out, but the next page holds the shape: Table 9, Table 4, Table 1, a time, and the word kitchen. The customer was Elena Cross. I’ve kept it with the takings.
calls.note: Nina Petrov has Elena Cross’s notebook; the page beneath a torn one shows Table 9, Table 4, Table 1, a time, and kitchen.

calls.label: Ask about the dinner she said no to
calls.player: Has anyone asked you out lately?
calls.reply: A widower from the casino’s board, Terence Ash. He wanted one honest meal before the club’s. I said I was tired. A lady from the club is planning to marry him, they say. I didn’t want to be the honest meal.
calls.note: Nina Petrov says the casino widower Terence Ash is expected to marry into the club.

women.name: Jessica Rivera
women.look: Olive skin, rose-gold bob, a beauty mark above her lip, striped T-shirt dress

own.label: Ask what the pharmacy is like
own.player: What’s it like working in a pharmacy?
own.reply: People tell me things they wouldn’t tell their doctor while I find their ointment. I know half of Sunfall’s secrets and all of its rashes.

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: You sing in a choir?
own.reply: Second soprano, hidden at the back. I mouth the high notes. Nobody has noticed in four years, or they’re too polite to say.

own.label: Ask if she’s shy or just careful
own.player: Are you shy, or just careful?
own.reply: Both. I rehearse phone calls in the shower. I once said you too to a waiter who told me to enjoy my meal. I still think about it.

own.label: Ask what she’d do if she weren’t scared
own.player: What would you do if you weren’t scared?
own.reply: Sing a solo. Just once. Loud, at the front, with everyone looking. Then probably faint.

own.label: Ask how she got the job
own.player: How did you end up at the pharmacy?
own.reply: My uncle’s a pharmacist and got me in. Dad fixes the museum’s lifts, Mum runs the parish school office. A very quiet family. I fit right in.

own.label: Ask about rehearsing calls
own.player: Do you really rehearse phone calls?
own.reply: In the shower, every time. I once said you too to a waiter who told me to enjoy my meal. I still think about it at night.

calls.label: Ask what the lodge’s van collects
calls.player: What does the van from the ridge pick up?
calls.reply: Every night with no moon: burn dressings, sutures, sedatives on a prescription from a doctor I’ve never seen. Once a veterinary tranquilliser we don’t stock, ordered in from a vet in the city. I copy the prescriptions. I’m quiet. I copy things.
calls.note: Jessica Rivera says the lodge’s van collects burn dressings, sutures, sedatives and once a veterinary tranquilliser on moonless nights.

women.name: Alana Brooks
women.look: Deep brown skin, honey-blonde beach waves, a silver ear cuff, mint polo shirt

own.label: Ask about the museum
own.player: What’s it like working at the museum?
own.reply: Quiet, cool and full of things people loved enough to keep. I tell school groups not to touch, and then I let the shy kids touch one thing.

own.label: Ask about her cookbooks
own.player: I hear you collect strange cookbooks?
own.reply: A church fundraiser book from the fifties with eleven recipes for jelly salad. Every family in it is listed by name. It’s the best history of Sunfall I own.

own.label: Ask what’s worrying her
own.player: Something on your mind?
own.reply: A woman who used to clean at the museum saw something on the gala night and told me. Now she tells everyone she was home all night. People don’t forget like that. They get frightened like that.
own.note: Alana Brooks says a museum cleaner who saw something on gala night now claims she was home all night.

own.label: Ask what she’d put in a museum of her life
own.player: What would go in a museum of your life?
own.reply: A burnt pan, a library card, and a letter I never sent. The letter would be the main exhibit.

own.label: Ask about her cookbook shelf
own.player: What’s on your cookbook shelf?
own.reply: A Victorian guide to feeding forty and a wartime pamphlet on cactus. Mum’s cookbooks went in the fire, so I’m rebuilding the shelf. It’s the only thing I have that keeps getting bigger.

own.label: Ask about her sisters
own.player: Are you the eldest Brooks?
own.reply: Eldest of four, plus two cousins. I do weekends at the diner and weekdays at the museum. I sign for every loan that comes through the museum door. Lately I wonder what I’m signing.

calls.label: Ask about the night of the fire
calls.player: What happened the night the diner burned?
calls.reply: The file says it started in the fryer. The fryer was off. I turned it off myself. And the private booking that night was for nine.
calls.note: Alana Brooks says the Lucky Cactus fire that killed her mother can’t have started in the fryer: she had turned it off, and the private booking that night was for nine.

women.name: Samantha Price
women.look: Warm beige skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, a tiny scar through one eyebrow, mint polo shirt

women.name: Jade Carter
women.look: Waifish and slight, a slim small-busted figure, pale freckled skin, wide-set grey eyes with a sleepy sullen gaze, a gap-toothed smile, golden-brown ringlets, an oversized yellow sundress

women.name: Karina Flores
women.look: Slight and narrow-shouldered, pale freckled skin, wide-set heavy-lidded eyes, a strong nose, an ash-blonde lob, a sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask what tourists ask her
own.player: What do tourists ask you?
own.reply: Whether the cacti are real, whether the desert is always this hot and whether I’m single. Yes, yes, and it depends on the tip.

own.label: Ask what her book club reads
own.player: What does your book club read?
own.reply: Thrillers where the husband did it. Every time. We’re a very suspicious book club. Two members have since divorced.

own.label: Ask about Sunfall’s best-kept secret
own.player: What’s Sunfall’s best-kept secret?
own.reply: A hot spring past the old drive-in, behind a fence that says no entry. Nobody checks. I only take people there off the books.

own.label: Ask if she’d ever leave Sunfall
own.player: Would you ever leave Sunfall?
own.reply: I show people this town every day, so I know how small it is. Still, I keep finding new corners. Maybe I’m waiting for a reason to stay.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Have you got family in town?
own.reply: My sister Bernadette at the museum, my cousin Gina at the Daily. Dad built the museum’s display cases and married Mum at St Brigid’s. We’re a family of people who look after old things.

own.label: Ask about her tour route
own.player: Where does the tour go?
own.reply: Casino, canyon, the Old Mission, the reservoir, the Cemetery Chapel. I wrote the script. There’s a second script in my head I don’t say out loud.

calls.label: Ask what the second script is
calls.player: What’s in the script you don’t say aloud?
calls.reply: At the Cemetery Chapel I tell the tourists the angels face the desert. In my head I’m counting the stones with blue ribbons and their dates. I’ve walked it forty times. I could recite them.
calls.note: Karina Flores knows every blue-ribboned grave at the Cemetery Chapel and its date.

women.name: Molly Sutton
women.look: Light olive skin, rose-gold bob, a small nose stud, sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask what reception is like
own.player: What’s it like working on reception?
own.reply: I say good morning about three hundred times a day. I mean it every time, which I think scares people.

own.label: Ask about her cactus garden
own.player: How many cacti do you have?
own.reply: Forty-one. They all have names. Gerald is the big one. He’s had a hard year. We don’t talk about the incident with the cat.

own.label: Ask if she talks a lot
own.player: Do you always talk this much?
own.reply: Only when I’m nervous. And happy. And bored. Okay, yes. But I’m a very good listener too, I promise. Go on. Your turn.

own.label: Ask what she wishes people knew
own.player: What do you wish people knew about you?
own.reply: That I’m not as silly as I sound. I notice who’s having a bad day before they’ve said a word. I just say good morning extra nicely to them.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Who do you live with?
own.reply: My big sister Phoebe. She cooks, pays the bills and is asleep by ten. She ran our house from fourteen and ran me too. I talk enough for both of us.

own.label: Ask what she says on the phone
own.player: What do you say when you answer the phone?
own.reply: Blue Ribbon Foundation, Scholarship Drive office, how may I help. Three hundred times a day, and I mean it every time, which I think scares people.

calls.label: Ask about the visitors’ book
calls.player: Who visits the committee room?
calls.reply: I write everyone in a book, because Phoebe taught me to. A man in a lanyard goes up to the committee room without signing. He’s in my book eleven times, no surname. I call him the tall gentleman. Mr Kell calls him Marchbanks.
calls.note: Molly Sutton’s visitors’ book has Marchbanks, the tall gentleman, going up to the committee room unsigned eleven times.
